block_summary_target: The cardiac-conventions lesson introduces parasternal long-axis orientation using a heart model and screen-marker diagrams. Narration pairs a right-sided screen marker with a probe marker toward the patient’s right shoulder, and a left-sided screen marker with a probe marker toward the left hip. Both arrangements are described as obtaining a long-axis heart section.
global_summary_target: The lesson begins by relating cardiac screen-marker location to transducer orientation. For parasternal long-axis imaging, right-screen-marker/right-shoulder and left-screen-marker/left-hip configurations are illustrated, followed by an oblique long-axis heart section.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The lesson introduces cardiac ultrasound conventions with a title slide containing a B-mode cardiac example. Narration states that the module will examine commonly used cardiac imaging conventions in more detail.

The acknowledgment slide credits MGH emergency-ultrasound images and CURE; the image then transitions to a heart model over a torso with a vertical arrow. The transcript contains an incomplete reference to a prior tutorial, so it is omitted.

A heart-in-thorax diagram changes from a vertical axis to a diagonal axis labeled R Shoulder and L Hip. Narration discusses parasternal long-axis imaging and alternative transducer-marker directions, including toward the patient’s right shoulder.

A yellow arrow highlights the screen marker on the right side of the sector apex, beside a diagram labeled R Shoulder. Narration explains that a right-sided screen marker corresponds to pointing the transducer marker toward the patient’s right shoulder for this view.

The yellow arrow now highlights the screen marker to the left of the sector apex, and the thoracic diagram is labeled L Hip. Narration specifies pointing the transducer marker toward the patient’s left hip when using this left-sided screen-marker convention.
The heart model is shown close up and then partly sectioned along an oblique plane. Narration explains that both marker conventions obtain a long-axis section through the heart.

block_summary_target: A cutaway heart model is reoriented to match a parasternal long-axis sonogram. Narration relates the view to looking from the patient’s left and identifies the right ventricle, left ventricle with apex toward image left, left atrium and aortic outflow. The intact model then returns as another convention is introduced.
global_summary_target: The lesson compares cardiac marker conventions that produce similar parasternal long-axis views. Screen-marker/probe-marker relationships are illustrated, then a reoriented cutaway model is matched to the cardiac sonogram and its ventricular, atrial and outflow anatomy. A further convention is introduced at the end of this prefix.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The sectioned heart model is shown from a changed viewpoint with ventricular cavities and valve structures exposed. Narration describes rotating the section and imagining a viewpoint from the patient’s left side.

The cutaway heart retains exposed chambers and valves as the surrounding torso fades. Narration explains that the two conventions generate similar images when the section is viewed into the heart from the patient’s left side.

The sectioned heart is reoriented horizontally beside a parasternal long-axis B-mode example, with a probe illustration above it. The model and sonogram show ventricular and outflow structures; narration begins identifying the right ventricle.

A horizontal long-axis heart model is paired with a parasternal long-axis B-mode view. Narration identifies the left ventricle with its apex directed toward image left, the left atrium and the aortic outflow region.
The paired long-axis model and cardiac B-mode example remain briefly before the intact anterior heart model returns. Narration closes the comparison of the two previously described conventions.
An intact anterior heart model with great vessels remains on screen. Narration introduces an additional commonly used cardiac ultrasound convention beyond the two already discussed.

block_summary_target: The instructor demonstrates the same long-axis cardiac section viewed from the patient's right side. The model and matching parasternal long-axis sonogram place the apex on image right, with the right ventricle superiorly. Narration identifies the left atrium, aorta, aortic valve region, and mitral valve. A stacked comparison contrasts this orientation with the earlier apex-left view.
global_summary_target: This lesson compares cardiac ultrasound display conventions using heart models and parasternal long-axis sonograms. The instructor explains pairing a right-sided screen marker with the probe indicator toward the patient's right shoulder, or a left-sided screen marker with the indicator toward the left hip; both examples show the apex on image left. Viewing the same section from the patient's right produces an alternative apex-right image. Paired models and sonograms illustrate the ventricles, left atrium, aorta, and valve regions before a stacked comparison of the two orientations.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The heart is sectioned again along its long axis and shown from the opposite side, exposing the ventricular cavity and valve apparatus. Narration describes taking the same long-axis slice but viewing it from the patient’s right side.

The long-axis cutaway heart remains shown from the alternative viewpoint, with the ventricular apex toward lower image right. Narration contrasts looking into the heart from opposite sides of the patient.

The alternative cutaway orientation is placed beneath an illustrated transducer and blue beam beside a parasternal long-axis sonogram. The ventricular apex is oriented toward image right in the model and corresponding ultrasound example; narration presents the resulting convention.

The alternate parasternal long-axis sonogram and model place the left ventricle toward image right, while the right ventricular region remains near the top. Narration explains that the display reverses the previous left–right orientation.

The alternate long-axis cardiac image retains the ventricular apex toward image right. Narration identifies the left atrium, aorta and aortic valve region, while noting limited clarity of the valve in this example. A cutaway model and blue beam illustrate the same orientation.

The instructor points out the mitral valve region in the alternative parasternal long-axis view. The slide then stacks two heart models and corresponding sonograms, comparing a view with the apex on image left against one with the apex on image right.

block_summary_target: Stacked models and sonograms show mirror-opposite parasternal long-axis orientations. The instructor describes a left screen marker with the probe indicator toward the right shoulder for the apex-right view. An ACEP policy slide lists the left-hip direction and the right-shoulder alternative with the screen marker remaining on the left. The lesson then turns to choosing a convention.
global_summary_target: The lesson compares cardiac ultrasound conventions through heart sections and parasternal long-axis sonograms. Pairing a right screen marker with a probe indicator toward the patient's right shoulder, or a left screen marker with the indicator toward the left hip, produces the illustrated apex-left view. Looking at the same section from the patient's right produces an apex-right view; a left screen marker with the indicator toward the right shoulder illustrates this alternative. The instructor identifies ventricular, atrial, aortic, and valve regions, compares mirror-opposite displays, and cites an ACEP policy slide listing left-hip and right-shoulder probe-marker directions.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: Stacked heart models and parasternal long-axis sonograms compare apex-left and apex-right displays. The instructor explains that the two images depict nearly identical anatomy in mirror-opposite orientations.

The paired displays retain opposite left–right orientations. For the lower, apex-right view, the instructor specifies a screen marker on the left and a transducer indicator directed toward the patient's right shoulder.

The instructor considers either illustrated orientation reasonable. The next slide cites an ACEP ultrasound imaging policy and lists a left screen marker with the probe marker toward the patient's left hip, plus an alternative using the right shoulder.

An ACEP policy slide describes a left-sided screen marker with the probe indicator toward the patient's left hip. The instructor discusses this choice when the screen marker is not switched; the slide also lists the right-shoulder alternative.

The instructor associates the left-hip probe-marker direction with images resembling cardiology textbook views. The policy slide lists directing the probe marker toward the patient's right shoulder as an alternative while retaining a left-sided screen marker.

The instructor explains that the alternative probe-marker direction produces the opposite image orientation and raises the choice between conventions. The policy slide gives way to two parasternal long-axis sonograms with opposite left–right displays.

block_summary_target: The instructor discusses practical factors for choosing a cardiac display convention: familiarity for clinicians and trainees, the conventions used by cardiologists or emergency physicians with whom they communicate, and colleagues' ability to mentally reverse the image. Opposite-orientation parasternal long-axis sonograms illustrate the discussion before a heart-and-syringe diagram appears.
global_summary_target: Heart models and parasternal long-axis sonograms illustrate cardiac display conventions. Right-screen-marker/right-shoulder and left-screen-marker/left-hip pairings produce the illustrated apex-left image, whereas a left screen marker with the probe indicator toward the right shoulder gives the opposite orientation. The instructor compares the ventricular, atrial, aortic, and valve regions across these views and cites an ACEP slide listing left-hip and right-shoulder alternatives. Choosing a convention is discussed in terms of image familiarity, trainees, communication partners, and their ability to mentally reverse an unfamiliar display.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: Two parasternal long-axis sonograms retain opposite left–right orientations. The instructor suggests choosing a convention partly according to which image orientation clinicians and their trainees are accustomed to seeing.

The instructor argues for learning and teaching the convention that matches a familiar cardiac image orientation. The slide continues to compare two parasternal long-axis sonograms with opposite left–right displays.
The two cardiac sonograms remain side by side in opposite orientations. The instructor notes that familiarity with interpreting one display may make it easier to keep using that convention.

The instructor recommends understanding both cardiac image conventions and considering the colleagues with whom images are discussed within the institution. The sonogram comparison transitions to an illustrative physician name tag.

The instructor advises considering whether communication is mainly with cardiologists or emergency physicians, which display conventions they use, and whether they can flip images. The slide returns from a physician name tag to the paired opposite-orientation cardiac sonograms.

The instructor adds whether colleagues can mentally reverse an unfamiliar image orientation as a factor in choosing a cardiac convention. The visual comparison then changes to a heart-section diagram with a surrounding blue region, a probe above, and a syringe to the upper right.

block_summary_target: A heart-section, probe, and syringe diagram illustrates how procedural position and needle approach may make one display orientation more intuitive. The instructor relates the view from the patient's right to recognizing the probe marker and needle-tip entry side. Opposite diagrams show syringes approaching from opposite image sides. Mastering both conventions is recommended, followed by a reference to Chris Moore's 2008 article.
global_summary_target: The lesson uses heart sections and parasternal long-axis sonograms to compare cardiac display conventions. It explains screen-marker and probe-indicator pairings that produce apex-left or apex-right images, identifies the corresponding cardiac anatomy, and presents an ACEP slide listing left-hip and right-shoulder alternatives with a left screen marker. Choice is discussed in terms of familiarity, trainees, communication partners, and procedural position. Heart-and-syringe diagrams relate the display orientation to recognizing the probe marker and needle approach. The instructor recommends understanding both conventions and refers to Chris Moore's 2008 article for historical and technical discussion.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: A teaching diagram shows a cutaway heart surrounded by a blue region, with an ultrasound probe above and a syringe at the upper right. The instructor introduces how one image convention may be more intuitive than another for a procedure.

Using the heart-and-syringe teaching diagram, the instructor asks whether a view from the patient's right side matches the operator's position during a pericardial procedure. The probe is illustrated above the heart and the syringe approaches from the upper right.

The instructor relates the chosen view to recognizing the transducer marker and the side from which a needle tip approaches. The diagram switches between opposite heart orientations, with the syringe moving from the upper-right side of the image to the upper-left while the probe remains above.

The apex-left heart diagram shows a probe above the heart and a syringe directed toward it from the upper left. The instructor continues relating image orientation to the side from which the needle approaches.

The instructor recommends mastering both conventions. A reference slide presents Chris Moore's article, “Current Issues with Emergency Cardiac Ultrasound Probe and Image Conventions,” as further discussion of the differing probe and display conventions.

The reference slide displays Chris Moore's 2008 article on emergency cardiac ultrasound probe and image conventions. The instructor recommends it for the history of the differing approaches and a more detailed account of the conventions.

block_summary_target: The lesson moves from its reference article to chest photographs labeled PSLA and PSSA. The instructor explains obtaining parasternal short axis by a 90-degree clockwise probe rotation from long axis. The concluding paired heart sections and sonograms summarize the apex-left pairings: right screen marker with probe indicator toward the patient's right shoulder, or left screen marker with indicator toward the left hip.
global_summary_target: The lesson compares cardiac ultrasound conventions using heart sections and parasternal long-axis sonograms. It demonstrates marker pairings for apex-left and apex-right displays, relates ventricular, atrial, aortic, and valve anatomy across them, and presents an ACEP slide listing left-hip and right-shoulder alternatives with a left screen marker. Familiarity, communication, and procedural position guide the instructor's discussion of choosing a convention and recognizing needle approach; understanding both is recommended. Chest probe photographs illustrate parasternal long and short axis, with a narrated 90-degree clockwise rotation between them. The concluding comparison reiterates the right-screen/right-shoulder and left-screen/left-hip pairings for apex-left imaging.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The instructor notes that the discussion has focused on the confusing parasternal long-axis convention. The reference slide transitions to chest probe-placement photographs labeled PSLA and PSSA, with a probe illustration and diagonal double-headed arrow below.

Chest photographs labeled PSLA and PSSA appear above a probe diagram with a diagonal axis; the transcript begins describing rotation from the parasternal long-axis position. The two-heart comparison belongs outside this 10-second window and is omitted.

The instructor explains that rotating the probe 90 degrees clockwise from the parasternal long-axis position obtains a parasternal short-axis view. The slide shows PSLA and PSSA chest probe positions and an orange curved arrow around the illustrated probe.

The slide retains the PSLA and PSSA probe-placement examples and rotation diagram. The instructor contrasts the more confusing parasternal long-axis conventions with two common conventions for other cardiac views, mentioning apical four-chamber imaging.

The concluding comparison pairs apex-left and apex-right heart sections with their sonograms. Beside the apex-left example, the slide lists “Screen R / R shoulder” and “Screen L / L Hip,” summarizing two marker pairings for that display.

The instructor summarizes how to obtain the apex-left display: with the screen marker on the right, direct the probe indicator toward the patient's right shoulder; with the screen marker on the left, direct it toward the left hip. The paired models and sonograms illustrate both image orientations.

The instructor states that an apex-right image typically uses a left-sided screen marker. The slide adds “Screen L / R shoulder” beside the lower, apex-right heart model and sonogram, contrasting it with the apex-left pairings above.

The final comparison confirms the apex-right pairing of a left screen marker with the probe indicator toward the patient's right shoulder. Above it, the apex-left example retains the right-screen/right-shoulder and left-screen/left-hip pairings as the instructor closes the lesson.

block_summary_target: The lung examination begins with a curvilinear probe on the upper anterior chest; teaching text also permits a phased-array probe. Ribs, posterior shadows and pleural line are annotated in B-mode. The instructor discusses pneumothorax, effusion and consolidation as examination purposes and recommends a superficial anterior lawnmower scanning pattern before moving to the opposite side.
global_summary_target: The lesson introduces curvilinear lung ultrasound and demonstrates upper anterior-chest scanning. Annotated B-mode images identify ribs, their shadows and pleural line for sliding assessment. Narration describes a superficial lawnmower survey and moving to the opposite anterior chest, with pneumothorax, effusion and consolidation named as examination purposes.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: Narration introduces lung scanning with a curvilinear transducer for a broader field of view. A supine subject’s anterior chest is shown, and on-screen teaching text notes that a phased-array transducer may also be used.

The curved probe is placed on the upper anterior chest. B-mode shows superficial chest-wall layers, a rib interface with posterior shadowing and adjacent bright pleural-region echoes. The instructor introduces lung examination for pneumothorax or effusion as its clinical purpose.

The upper anterior-chest B-mode image is annotated with ribs, their posterior shadows and the pleural line. On-screen arrows identify the pleural region for sliding assessment. Narration adds consolidation to the examination purposes and describes orienting the probe indicator toward the head.

The instructor describes working down and across the anterior chest. The inset shows curvilinear-probe contact on the upper chest, while B-mode depicts rib shadows and a bright pleural interface between them; the teaching rib/pleural annotations appear early in the window.

Narration describes a lawnmower pattern for lung scanning and emphasizes the superficial target depth. The probe is shown at differing anterior-chest positions; B-mode retains rib shadows and bright pleural-region echoes.

The instructor moves to the other anterior-chest side and recommends starting high again. The inset shows probe placement near the upper chest/clavicular region; B-mode depicts superficial structures with posterior rib shadows and adjacent pleural-region echoes.

block_summary_target: Opposite-side anterior lung scanning shows rib shadows and pleural-region echoes while narration discusses sliding assessment and looking for B-lines. The instructor then increases depth for a lateral view. Teaching text specifies xiphoid-level placement at the mid-posterior axillary line with a 1–2 o’clock indicator; the lateral B-mode image labels spleen and diaphragm.
global_summary_target: The lung-ultrasound lesson demonstrates curvilinear anterior surveys with rib/pleural-line annotations and narrated assessment goals including pneumothorax, effusion, consolidation and B-lines. It then moves to deeper lateral scanning, with placement instructions at xiphoid level near the mid-posterior axillary line. The spleen and diaphragm are identified in the lateral B-mode teaching view.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The curvilinear probe is shown at different anterior-chest positions on the opposite side. B-mode depicts superficial chest wall, rib shadows and bright pleural-region echoes. Narration discusses identifying rib shadows and assessing sliding while surveying the lungs.

The probe continues across the anterior chest. A bright pleural-region line and rib shadows are seen in B-mode before the image briefly loses deeper tissue detail during repositioning. Narration discusses looking for B-lines as part of the lung examination.

The instructor recommends increasing imaging depth for lateral-lung assessment, mentioning approximately 17–18 as a depth setting before moving to the side. The displayed B-mode scale expands beyond 15, while the inset shows the anterior chest during repositioning.

The probe is placed on the lateral lower chest. On-screen instructions specify xiphoid level at the mid-posterior axillary line, with the indicator between 1 and 2 o’clock. Narration discusses raising the arm and adjusting probe orientation; the deep B-mode field is partly obscured by shadow.

The lateral thoracoabdominal view is annotated with spleen and a bright curved diaphragm interface. The curvilinear probe remains against the lateral lower chest, and narration recommends finding the diaphragm first.

The lateral B-mode view labels the spleen, kidney, spine and spine shadows. A yellow arrow marks the deep spinal echoes, while the curved probe remains against the lower lateral thoracoabdominal region.

block_summary_target: The lateral view is used to teach that spinal echoes stop at the diaphragm, with annotations explaining absent spine visibility above it. Narration attributes this to aerated-lung shadowing, then describes zigzag lateral scanning toward the axilla with pauses for sliding assessment. Excessive probe angulation is demonstrated as a cause of soft-tissue-only views.
global_summary_target: Curvilinear lung-ultrasound teaching progresses from superficial anterior surveys to deeper lateral scanning. Ribs, shadows, pleural line, spleen and diaphragm are identified in annotated examples. Narration discusses lung-sliding assessment, lawnmower/zigzag coverage and checking spinal visibility at the diaphragm. The instructor also illustrates how excessive angulation can produce chest-wall soft-tissue views rather than the intended lung window.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The lateral thoracoabdominal image shows solid organ tissue and kidney. Yellow arrows label the bright diaphragm, and separate teaching text states that the spine is not visible above the diaphragm. Narration describes spinal echoes stopping at the diaphragm.

The annotated lateral view repeats that the spine is not visible above the diaphragm. As the probe angle changes at the lower lateral chest, broad shadowing obscures much of the left image while abdominal tissue remains visible toward image right.

The instructor explains that aerated lung obscures spinal echoes and recommends a zigzag or lawnmower approach for lateral-lung examination. The probe is shown at successive lateral lower-chest positions, with B-mode alternating between visible abdominal tissue and broad acoustic shadowing.

The lateral-chest B-mode view shows a bright pleural interface beneath chest-wall layers, with deeper shadowing and reverberation. Yellow arrows label the region for sliding assessment. The instructor emphasizes checking sliding and rib shadows during the survey.

The probe is shown farther superiorly along the lateral chest toward the axilla. Narration recommends intermittent pauses to assess lung sliding during the survey. The B-mode field contains superficial chest-wall interfaces with predominantly dark deeper tissue due to shadowing.

The instructor warns that excessive probe angulation can show only chest-wall soft tissue rather than the intended thoracic view. The inset shows markedly altered probe angle at the lateral chest, while B-mode depicts layered soft tissue with poor pleural definition.

The demonstration switches from the lateral pleural view to the right lower thoracoabdominal region. The B-mode image shows homogeneous liver tissue with branching vessels and a bright curved diaphragmatic interface. Narration recommends identifying the diaphragm above the liver on the right side.

The right lower lateral B-mode view labels liver, diaphragm, spine and spine shadows, with arrows marking the diaphragm and spinal echoes. Narration describes spinal echoes stopping at the diaphragm; the probe remains at the right lower lateral thoracoabdominal region.

The right lateral probe position is adjusted to display a superficial bright pleural-region interface with reverberation and dark deeper field. Narration recommends assessing pleural sliding at the top of this view.

The probe remains on the right lateral chest. A yellow arrow marks a narrow bright vertical artifact extending below the pleural line. Narration identifies a single B-line and describes checking sliding from anterior to posterior.

The lateral chest survey continues toward the axilla. B-mode shows chest-wall layers and a bright interface labeled sliding pleural line, with two arrows marking it above a largely dark deeper field. The inset shows upper lateral chest probe contact.

global_summary_target: The lecture progresses from infraclavicular transverse and long-axis vessel views to Doppler, needle visualization and wire confirmation. It discusses the pleural line and intended wire path, then transitions toward research comparing scan approaches.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: A long-axis ultrasound view shows a pulsatile vessel; the narration recommends Doppler confirmation.

block_summary_target: The lesson reviews needle tracking near the vessel and pleural line, then presents a study comparing long- and short-axis views. A long-axis advantage slide is followed by ultrasound wire-confirmation images and a transition to the supraclavicular approach.
global_summary_target: The video demonstrates ultrasound-guided subclavian access with transverse and long-axis views, Doppler, needle tracking and wire confirmation. The presenters review long-axis versus short-axis evidence and introduce the supraclavicular approach and central-vein anatomy.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: A long-axis ultrasound image is paired with a skin-level needle demonstration.

block_summary_target: Wire-confirmation ultrasound images accompany advice to verify that the wire remains in the vessel and follows the intended route. The lesson then introduces supraclavicular anatomy, including the internal jugular, subclavian and brachiocephalic veins.
global_summary_target: The lecture demonstrates infraclavicular ultrasound and wire confirmation, then introduces supraclavicular access. Diagrams trace the internal jugular and subclavian veins into the brachiocephalic vein, and the presenters discuss probe placement and needle-guidance views.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The slide lists shorter cannulation time, fewer redirections and fewer posterior-wall penetrations.

The wire is shown as a bright linear structure within the vessel lumen in a long-axis view.

block_summary_target: The supraclavicular section combines vascular diagrams, probe demonstrations and ultrasound images. It presents linear-probe options and describes following the internal jugular to its junction with the subclavian vein before showing a longitudinal needle-guidance approach.

block_summary_target: The lesson introduces ultrasound-guided supraclavicular regional nerve block using a linear-array transducer. B-mode examples show a round dark vessel beside smaller hypoechoic structures, while torso and exposed anatomical illustrations demonstrate probe placement above the clavicle. The narration gives a 1–3 cm target-depth estimate, recommends a 45-degree reclining position with the operative neck exposed and head turned away, and describes an oblique probe position posterior to the clavicular midpoint with the marker toward the patient's right near 10 o'clock. A green-ringed vessel is identified by the narration as the subclavian artery; pulsatility is a narrated characteristic.
global_summary_target: So far, the supraclavicular block lesson has established the linear-format ultrasound appearance and illustrated how the probe relates to the clavicle, nearby vessels and nerve structures. The narrated preparation covers reclining/head position, an estimated superficial target depth, and oblique probe/marker alignment toward the thorax. The first explicitly identified ultrasound landmark is the round subclavian artery, highlighted in green and described as pulsatile by the narration.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: A title introduces ultrasound-guided supraclavicular regional nerve block. A transverse linear-format B-mode image shows a rounded anechoic vessel beside smaller hypoechoic structures, with bright deep interfaces and acoustic shadows; an anatomical inset shows the probe near the clavicle. The narration introduces a linear-array transducer.

The supraclavicular B-mode example shows a rounded dark vessel adjacent to a cluster of smaller hypoechoic structures, above bright deep interfaces and shadowing. The anatomical inset places the probe over the clavicular region. The narration describes the regional block and gives an approximate target depth of 1–3 cm as a procedural teaching estimate.

A supraclavicular B-mode example with a dark vessel and adjacent smaller hypoechoic structures transitions to a torso-model view showing the probe at the lower lateral neck above the clavicular region. The narration recommends a 45-degree reclining position, a pillow beneath the head and exposure of the operative side of the neck.

The probe-on-neck illustration transitions to an exposed anatomical view of the clavicular region, adjacent vessels and nerve structures beneath the probe's illustrated ultrasound beam. The narration recommends turning the head to the opposite side and begins landmark identification of the supraclavicular brachial plexus.

An exposed clavicular/vessel/nerve illustration gives way to the probe resting obliquely over the supraclavicular region, with a green clock-face orientation graphic. The narration places the transducer posterior to the clavicle's midpoint at an acute angle and directs the marker toward the patient's right, approximately the 10-o'clock position.

An oblique probe and clock-face orientation graphic give way to an exposed thoracic/clavicular anatomical view beneath the probe, then a transverse B-mode image with a green ring around a round anechoic vessel. The narration directs the transducer toward the thorax and identifies the highlighted vessel as the subclavian artery, describing it as pulsatile.

block_summary_target: The supraclavicular B-mode lesson highlights the first-rib reflection beneath the artery, the pleural reflection and a cluster of small hypoechoic nerve trunks in brighter tissue beside the vessel. The narration explains these landmarks, recommends Doppler to identify small arterial branches and describes a lateral, in-plane needle approach. A bright oblique needle echo and later dark fluid-like pockets appear beside the nerve region, with a matching anatomical needle/syringe illustration. The narrated initial endpoint is posterior to the artery above the first rib; distinguishing pleura from rib, pneumothorax avoidance, incremental local-anesthetic injection and possible redirection toward upper trunks are discussed.
global_summary_target: The lesson has progressed from supraclavicular block setup and oblique linear-probe placement to ultrasound landmark identification and an illustrated in-plane needle approach. B-mode examples and green overlays distinguish a round artery, adjacent hypoechoic nerve trunks, bright rib/pleural interfaces and later needle echoes and fluid-like pockets near the plexus region. The narration supplies patient/probe positioning, estimated depths and lateral entry distance, Doppler assessment of smaller vessels, a first-rib-related needle endpoint, pleural precautions and incremental injection technique. These are narrated teaching steps; clinical block success and actual drug identity are not established by the sampled images.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The round anechoic vessel lies above a bright interface with deep shadowing; a green overlay highlights this interface, then a deeper bright line toward image-right. The narration identifies the first-rib reflection beneath the artery and describes the pleural reflection as bright and at or deeper than the rib's level.

Green spots highlight a cluster of small rounded structures immediately to image-right of the round anechoic artery in the transverse B-mode view, with corresponding nerve anatomy in the inset. The narration identifies these as brachial-plexus nerve trunks and describes them as hypoechoic dark circles.

The grayscale transverse view continues to show small hypoechoic nerve-region structures in brighter surrounding tissue beside the round artery, with an anatomical inset. The narration describes the bright brachial-plexus fascia and recommends Doppler imaging to identify smaller arterial branches through the plexus; no Doppler flow display is shown in these frames.

The initial grayscale landmark view is followed by a B-mode view with an oblique bright needle echo approaching the plexus-region from image-right; the anatomical inset illustrates a needle approaching beside the probe toward the nerve bundle. The narration specifies an entry 1–2 cm lateral to the transducer and an in-plane advancement technique.

An oblique echogenic needle shaft is visible beneath the plexus-region beside the round artery, with a syringe/needle trajectory in the anatomical inset. A later B-mode image shows a dark fluid-like pocket adjacent to the nerve region. The narration places the intended initial endpoint just posterior to the artery above the first rib and emphasizes distinguishing pleura from rib.

The B-mode view shows dark fluid-like areas around the hypoechoic nerve region beside the artery, with a needle/syringe anatomical inset. The narration mentions pneumothorax avoidance, describes incremental local-anesthetic injection close to the nerves and discusses redirecting the needle toward upper nerve trunks; the final anatomical phrase is truncated in the window ASR.

The presentation examines the pulmonary-vein Doppler waveform, including systolic and diastolic waves and their relation to left-atrial pressure and mitral regurgitation. The lecture then returns to an apical four-chamber simulator view to discuss right-ventricular size and function, the tricuspid valve and right atrium, and positions an M-mode cursor. A slide lists lesion size and location, lesion visibility, imaging availability, and operator experience as imaging-selection factors. A slide states that lesions well visualized on sonography may be suitable for ultrasound-guided intervention. The strengths slide lists real-time guidance, speed, compression, and rapid complication checks; paired images show a sonogram and a procedure. Color Doppler and sonographic images illustrate ultrasound guidance. A real-time ultrasound example is shown beside the slide on intervention advantages. Slides and sonograms illustrate multiple-plane guidance and color Doppler vessel visualization. A slide separates diagnostic sampling from therapeutic procedures such as drainage, ablation, and vascular access. A procedure-room slide shows the room and monitoring equipment. A biopsy-preparation slide lists pre-procedure checks, coagulation, antibiotics, medication, and IV access. Guideline tables for checking coagulation disorders remain on screen. Slides show cleaning and preparing an ultrasound probe. A patient-preparation example is shown. A free-hand slide pairs the technique label with a probe and needle demonstration. Probe-guide examples are followed by a pelvic collection sonogram labeled for guide use. Slides state that poor needle-tip visibility commonly follows misalignment and that the lesion, needle, and central beam should share a plane. A diagram contrasts needle and beam alignment relative to the target. The in-plane approach is demonstrated with a probe and needle on a patient. A needle guide and sonographic example illustrate the in-plane path. A slide notes that in-plane insertion shows the needle along its path, though it traverses more tissue. The out-of-plane approach is demonstrated; accompanying slides note that the needle is not visible along its full length. FNA examples compare in-plane visualization of the needle with out-of-plane visualization of its tip. A slide introduces tips for improving needle visualization. The slide lists alignment, shallow insertion angle, bevel rotation, smooth motion, and needle movement as visualization aids. Sonograms compare needle appearance; slides mention color flow and an echogenic needle. An ultrasound image is labeled as an example of a well-visualized needle. Needle-selection slides show several needle sizes and types. A slide introduces capillary-filling and syringe techniques for FNA. A capillary-filling slide shows probe and needle placement during aspiration. A syringe-assisted FNA slide shows needle movement and aspiration technique. A slide advises sampling the viable solid or peripheral portion of a lesion and handling cystic components separately. Slides and procedural stills show smear preparation, slide fixing, and labeling. An automated spring-loaded biopsy gun is shown. A slide lists core-biopsy gun advantages, including a larger core and single-pass sampling.

A Fascia Iliaca Plane Block slide and hip-fracture standard-of-care slide followed; the latter added pain control, one-year ambulation, and ‘< PNA, UTI and LOS.’ A labeled fascia iliaca cross-section gave way to an embedded LEFT HIP ultrasound with a diagonal needle-like line. Popliteal Sciatic indications and labeled probe/ultrasound examples followed, then a Serratus Anterior Plane Block slide with anterolateral chest, T2–T9, and a torso map. Research screenshots addressed mastectomy, thoracoscopic surgery, and rib fractures. Later samples showed lateral-chest probe-placement photos and a labeled chest cross-section with latissimus, serratus, ribs and pleura. In the current minute, that cross-section changes to an annotated serratus ultrasound with a probe-placement photo, then paired ultrasound panels illustrate an anterior fascial plane, needle graphic, white dots, pleural line and rib shadow. Attributed narration discusses serratus landmarks and placing injection above the muscle. The serratus ultrasound diagram remains into the next minute; at 1465 it changes to an Erector Spinae Plane Block slide with shaded back and chest-wall photos and printed indications for posterior rib fractures, chest or abdominal wall injury, and vertebral compression fracture, plus a 3–4 dermatome spread statement. Attributed narration introduces this posterior block. The Erector Spinae indication slide persists through the early current samples; by 1525, a two-panel image shows a covered probe placed beside the spine and an ultrasound labeled trapezius, rhomboid, erector spinae, transverse process (TP) and PVS. The image remains through 1559. Attributed narration discusses locating muscle layers and bony landmarks. The two-panel erector spinae probe-placement photo and labeled ultrasound remain visible into this minute. At 1589 a center inset appears, showing gloved hands with a green-tipped needle or device near the back while the ultrasound labels remain. Attributed narration discusses the transverse process and needle approach. The three-part erector spinae instructional image remains through 1659, with a back probe photo, gloved hands holding a green-tipped needle or device, and labeled ultrasound layers. At 1661 it changes to a Median/Radial/Ulnar slide with color-coded palmar and dorsal hand maps and a forearm photo marking the three nerve paths. Attributed narration shifts from erector spinae spread toward upper-limb blocks. The Median/Radial/Ulnar distribution graphic remains visible across the 1681–1739s samples, with color-coded palmar and dorsal hand maps and a forearm path image. Attributed narration discusses severe hand injuries and coordination with surgical consultants. The Median/Radial/Ulnar chart stays through 1765s, followed by adjacent views of a masked clinician and portable ultrasound unit at 1769–1771s, packaged supplies laid on gray at 1775–1785s, and the Median Nerve slide from 1789s, with a wrist probe image by 1795s. Attributed narration discusses hand specialist consultation, equipment, and median nerve territory. The median-nerve illustration labels the nerve and fascial plane beside a yellow hand map. A needle-labeled ultrasound overlay appears intermittently from 1829 through 1845 seconds. At 1849 seconds a “Radial Nerve” title replaces it; by 1859 seconds a red-highlighted dorsal hand territory is shown. Attributed narration describes median-nerve appearance and needle placement beside it. The wrist-probe image beside the red radial hand-territory map remains through 1881 seconds. At 1885 seconds it changes to an ultrasound labeled Radius, Radial Nerve and Radial Artery; by 1909 seconds a second panel labels a needle approach next to the nerve. Attributed narration discusses identifying the radial nerve near the artery and placing the needle alongside it. The radial needle-path ultrasound remains at 1921s; an Ulnar Nerve hand-territory slide appears by 1925s, a wrist-probe and syringe image by 1935s, an ulnar artery/nerve/fascial-plane ultrasound by 1941s, and a needle-labeled panel by 1949s. At 1959s the slide changes to Supraclavicular Brachial Plexus, saying “Entire arm... except the axilla” beside arm and shoulder illustrations. Attributed narration moves from radial/ulnar blocks to supraclavicular coverage. The supraclavicular brachial plexus slide stating “Entire arm... except the axilla” remains at 1981–2005 seconds, with a brief blank sharing screen at 1995 seconds. By 2009 seconds it changes to a NYSORA cross-sectional illustration labeling the subclavian artery, brachial plexus fascicles, first rib, pleura, and surrounding muscles, with two drawn needle trajectories. Attributed narration discusses the block’s arm coverage and anatomy above the clavicle. The NYSORA supraclavicular cross-section remains through 2049 seconds, labeling the subclavian artery, first rib, pleura and muscles around the brachial plexus. At 2051 seconds it changes to an annotated ultrasound labeled BP (brachial plexus), MSM (middle scalene muscle), SA (subclavian artery), 1st Rib and Pleura. A single blue needle-path arrow appears by 2079 seconds; a second blue arrow is visible at 2099 seconds. Attributed narration discusses identifying the artery and plexus and planning injections.

block_summary_target: The instructor introduces ultrasound-guided shoulder nerve-injection teaching, with the nerve name corrupted in ASR. global_summary_target: The first minute covers preparation for ultrasound-guided shoulder nerve-injection teaching: palpation of the scapular spine, posterior-shoulder linear-probe placement, and narrated adjustment of frequency and depth to include the scapula. The later close B-mode view shows layered tissue above a bright deep cortical interface. The exact nerve name remains uncertain in the ASR, and needle guidance or injection has not yet been shown.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The instructor introduces ultrasound-guided nerve-injection teaching, with the nerve name imperfectly transcribed as “super scapular.” A seated person’s posterior shoulder is exposed; the instructor palpates the scapular-spine region while holding a linear probe nearby. No readable sonographic anatomy or needle placement is shown yet.

The instructor continues palpating the posterior scapular landmark with the linear probe held beside the shoulder, then turns attention toward the ultrasound screen. The narration describes identifying the landmark by palpation. The distant display shows superficial echoes but does not yet permit confident anatomical identification.

The instructor recommends lowering the imaging frequency and says this machine goes down to eight. The camera faces the ultrasound unit, whose B-mode image shows superficial soft-tissue layers; the small distant display does not independently confirm the exact frequency or a specific nerve.

The linear probe contacts the posterior shoulder while the instructor adjusts the ultrasound unit. B-mode shows layered soft tissue, although the filmed screen remains small. Narration explains using lower frequency for deeper structures and setting sufficient depth to include the scapular bone, usually around four or slightly deeper on this machine.

A close external view shows the linear probe contacting the posterior upper shoulder, with its long footprint approximately transverse across the scapular region. The instructor explains keeping the transducer parallel to the scapular spine and scanning outward. The first sample is obscured, and no sonographic anatomy is readable in these views.

The camera moves closer to a B-mode shoulder image showing layered soft tissue and a deep bright sloping bony interface with darker tissue beyond it. The instructor freezes the view and begins identifying the cortex, with the anatomical word cut off in this window’s ASR. A finger points toward the deeper interface.

block_summary_target: The instructor uses the deep sloping cortical contour and its dip as a sonographic landmark, describing a ligament above the nerve and a planned steroid placement in that region. These small structures are narrated rather than confidently resolved on the filmed display. The probe remains at the posterior shoulder while narration discusses a 22-gauge spinal needle, positioning the landmark to one image side, and an in-plane approach. No actual needle placement or injection is established in this minute.
global_summary_target: Teaching has progressed from scapular-spine palpation and posterior-shoulder linear-probe positioning to B-mode landmark selection and a planned in-plane nerve injection. The filmed display shows layered tissue above a sloping deep cortical contour with a dip. The instructor describes the nerve beneath a ligament, steroid placement near it, and a preference for a 22-gauge spinal needle; exact nerve naming remains corrupted in ASR. At this point no needle entry or injectate spread has been established visually.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: A finger traces the deep sloping bright cortical contour on the B-mode display, including a lower dip. The filmed image does not independently resolve a distinct nerve or ligament with confidence.

The instructor points to the deep cortical dip on the displayed B-mode image and explains that this landmark must be visible before injection. Narration describes a planned needle path toward that region for steroid placement, with the ending phrase corrupted. The screen shows anatomical teaching without a visible procedural needle or injectate.

The B-mode shoulder image remains on screen before the camera returns to the linear probe contacting the posterior shoulder. The instructor says the intended placement is around the nerve and announces returning to live imaging; the nerve name is again transcribed as “super scapular” and remains flagged for listening.

The linear probe remains against the posterior shoulder as the instructor discusses a preference for a 22-gauge spinal needle because the target is relatively deep. The external view shows probe contact and nearby skin preparation; the needle gauge and target depth are narrated, with no demonstrated needle insertion in these samples.

The probe remains on the posterior shoulder while B-mode is visible at a distance. The instructor describes moving the cortical “ski-slope” dip toward one side of the image for the planned approach. The external view establishes probe contact but does not resolve a needle or allow precise image-side localization of the target.

The instructor describes an in-plane technique in which the needle will align with the ultrasound imaging plane. The external view shows the linear probe contacting the posterior shoulder; it does not show a clear needle shaft, skin entry, or sonographic needle path in these samples.

The probe remains on the posterior shoulder, and a syringe-mounted long needle is brought from camera right toward the skin beside the probe footprint. The instructor warns that a small pinch may be felt. The external view shows the approach near the skin but cannot confirm the deeper needle-tip position or injection.

The external view shows the syringe-mounted needle directed from camera right toward the skin immediately beside the probe, followed by the B-mode display of soft tissue over the deeper bright contour. The instructor offers brief reassurance. The filmed sonogram does not clearly establish the needle tip or a fluid deposit in these samples.

The B-mode display shows superficial tissue, deeper muscle-like layers, and a dark region near the deep bright cortical contour. The instructor says the medicine will inflate the area. The filmed stills do not clearly establish needle-tip location or dynamic injectate spread, so the inflation remains a narrated claim.

B-mode continues to show layered posterior-shoulder soft tissue over the deeper bright cortical contour; the displayed frequency reads 8.0 MHz. The image is filmed obliquely and does not clearly resolve a needle tip or permit a confident claim of fluid spread. This window’s ASR contains no text.

The camera moves away from the ultrasound display; an intermediate external view still shows the probe contacting the posterior shoulder before the clinician/practice closing card. The repeated final ASR phrase is unclear and supplies no reliable additional procedural information. The sampled ending does not establish the final needle position or treatment outcome.

The final recommendation is cut off. The angle-of-incidence lesson continues: shallow approaches may improve needle visibility but can be impractical for deep targets, while steep approaches may produce only a subtle shadow or tissue displacement instead of a bright tip. A slide introduces the vanishing bullseye, also called the advanced target sign. The instructor presents it as a technique to use after entering the vessel.
The schematic shows a needle advancing toward the red vessel lumen; the instructor says to follow the tip and avoid advancing through the far wall.
The teaching diagram places a dot inside the vessel as a bullseye. The instructor describes lowering the hand to center the target before making it vanish.
The schematic keeps the target dot within the vessel as the probe is moved away and tilted slightly. The instructor describes repeating the target-alignment maneuver.

block_summary_target: The segment moves from a diagram of the vanishing-bullseye maneuver to a hands-on vessel-access demonstration on a training model. The sonogram shows a dark lumen whose contour changes and rebounds across the sampled frames while the instructor describes tenting, entry, and following the needle tip. He then lowers and stabilizes the needle hand and begins removing the syringe. These narrated steps are instructional, not a patient outcome.
global_summary_target: The lecture introduces ultrasound-guided central venous access, its objectives, and the difference between assisted landmark-style access and guided needle localization. It then turns to vessel selection, labels the internal jugular vein and common carotid artery, and lists jugular, subclavian, and femoral sites. Study slides compare site-related infection, thrombosis, and mechanical complications and contrast ultrasound-guided with landmark subclavian access. The Vessel Options slides describe subclavian access as having the lowest CLABSI rate but higher hematoma risk, femoral access as having the highest DVT risk but lower mechanical-complication risk, and jugular access as intermediate. The lecture then introduces probe control for central-line ultrasound: a mannequin demonstration contrasts an elevated, unsupported probe hold with a hand anchored against the patient and probe contact, and describes a brief look-away as a steadiness check. The instructor further explains that probe stability helps prevent the target from shifting during local anesthetic injection. Animated diagrams compare gel-separated probe positioning with direct contact and contrast lighter with heavier pressure; he warns that excessive pressure can compress veins. A right internal jugular ultrasound example follows, with the instructor describing pressure-related collapse, though the sampled frames do not independently establish that dynamic change. The next sequence continues the right-IJV teaching example and warns that excess probe pressure can make vessels harder to see. A “Needle Tip Visualization — Hide and Seek” section follows: a schematic pairs a probe and needle with a grayscale display, while the instructor explains that an out-of-plane needle appears as a dot that disappears when the beam moves beyond the tip and reappears when it returns. The needle-tip section continues from the schematic into transverse and longitudinal vascular ultrasound examples. The instructor emphasizes that a moving echogenic dot may represent the needle shaft rather than the tip, warns against advancing when the tip is not visualized, and describes the out-of-plane hide-and-seek maneuver of moving the beam until the dot disappears and returns. The sampled frames do not confirm needle position or vessel puncture. The instructor then introduces needle angle of incidence as another factor in tip visualization. Diagrams compare a perpendicular 90° needle-to-beam alignment with increasingly steep trajectories labeled 64°, 32°, and 30°. The explanation attributes reduced tip visibility at steep angles to more sound energy being reflected away from the probe; an entry point close to the probe is shown producing a steep path. The final recommendation is cut off. The angle-of-incidence lesson continues: shallow approaches may improve needle visibility but can be impractical for deep targets, while steep approaches may produce only a subtle shadow or tissue displacement instead of a bright tip. A schematic compares the angle cases, then a hands-on tissue-model demonstration appears with an inset ultrasound view where the needle is not clearly visible in sampled frames. A final teaching slide pairs an ultrasound image with a beam-reflection diagram and research citation. The lecture next presents echogenic needles and beam steering as ways to improve the angle of incidence and needle visibility. Slides pair ultrasound examples showing bright linear echoes with reflection diagrams; notches are described as helping return sound toward the probe, and beam steering is illustrated as another way to approach a 90° angle. The sequence then introduces a practical bevel-orientation tip, showing a needle and syringe and instructing the viewer to align the bevel with the syringe numbers so visible numbers indicate the bevel is up. The next slide warns not to overtighten the needle on the syringe, since removing the syringe can otherwise move the needle. A title introduces a target-vessel survey, followed by a probe-orientation demonstration showing a linear probe at the neck beside an ultrasound display. The instructor stresses confirming left-right orientation and keeping the vessel centered; the sampled display does not clearly establish a particular vessel or finding. The lecture then demonstrates surveying a neck vessel: advance the linear probe along the vessel while keeping it centered on the ultrasound display, and assess patency. A colored schematic illustrates how an off-axis probe can make the vessel appear to shift side to side; the instructor compares alignment to following a railroad track and recommends practicing before needle insertion. A red X marks an incorrect position as a troubleshooting tip begins. These are teaching instructions, not patient-specific findings. The instructor continues with practical probe alignment: keep the target vessel centered while advancing the probe, align the operator and planned needle path with the vessel axis, and place the monitor along the scanning plane. A red X marks a poor position in the schematic. The lecture then moves to a hands-on phantom demonstration, where a hand slowly moves a linear probe on a gel-covered surface while ultrasound shows a round anechoic vessel-like structure with a bright rim. The instructor stabilizes the hand with the little finger and controls the probe with the thumb, index, and middle fingers. The instructor then transitions from probe stabilization and centering on a phantom to a ‘Skin to Vessel’ section about selecting a needle entry site. Slides illustrate avoiding an entry immediately beside the probe for shallow targets and choosing a trajectory related to vessel depth, including an approximately 45-degree approach. The diagrams are instructional, not patient measurements or a live needle image. The instructor continues with needle-path planning. A schematic compares vertical and approximately 45-degree approaches, followed by an annotated ultrasound still labeling the right common carotid artery beside a large round vessel-like lumen. Red and yellow dotted paths illustrate alternative approaches; the instructor recommends aiming for the vein center and cautions against an approach from the opposite side of the artery. These are teaching overlays, not live needle motion. The instructor next discusses maintaining skin tension during needle entry, including using the hypothenar side of the probe hand for traction. A schematic compares an approximately 45-degree path with a steeper angle for better visibility; the instructor describes reacquiring the bright needle tip with probe movement, then returning to the intended access angle while watching the display. These remain teaching illustrations rather than live needle motion. The instructor then stresses checking and restoring the intended needle angle, followed by a hide-and-seek maneuver in which probe advancement makes the tip disappear before it is reacquired. The instructor notes that the tip may appear subtle or as a small shadow and can still be tracked when its screen location is known. The accompanying vessel and needle images are schematic teaching illustrations, not live patient findings. The instructor emphasizes maintaining probe contact while tracking the needle and restarting if an early attempt loses the tip. A schematic then shows the needle approaching a vessel with an indentation at its wall, illustrating tenting before entry. The instructor describes using tenting as a landmark when the tip is hard to see and moving the probe to keep it visible before access; this is instructional artwork rather than a patient-specific finding. The instructor then discusses advancing through the vessel wall: a slow, hesitant approach may compress the vessel, so he recommends a sufficiently steep, deliberate advance while avoiding a through-and-through path. Schematic images show the needle entering the illustrated vessel. He describes tenting as a landmark when the tip is not visible and says its disappearance, sometimes with a slight peak and syringe flash, can indicate entry. These are instructional graphics, not patient-specific findings. The instructor then cautions against immediately threading a wire after obtaining flash and recommends following the needle tip. He contrasts sliding the probe at a steady angle, which can help visualize the tip, with fanning, which changes the beam angle and can make the tip harder to see. The accompanying material is instructional slides and schematic graphics, not patient-specific imaging. The instructor then frames probe fanning as a selective technique, especially near the clavicle or when needle-tip tracking is difficult. He describes adjusting the probe toward a near-perpendicular angle and using a hide-and-seek motion to relocate the tip; the clavicle can limit movement during internal jugular access, making a return to a straight position useful. The visuals shift from explanatory schematics to a hands-on probe-positioning demonstration over a draped surface. The instructor now demonstrates vessel access on a training model, with a round dark lumen on the sonogram and a needle advanced while the probe is repositioned. The lumen contour appears indented with a bright echo near its upper margin; the instructor describes this as tenting, followed by entry and blood flash. The segment ends with a slide on successful access and losing blood return when disconnecting the needle. These are instructional demonstrations, not patient-specific findings. The instructor next reviews losing blood return after disconnecting the needle and difficulty passing a wire, including possible contact with the vessel's far wall. He introduces the vanishing bullseye (advanced target) technique: the diagrams show a needle approaching a red vessel and a target dot centered within its lumen, with probe adjustment used to make the target vanish. The slide and diagram are instructional, not patient-specific findings. The instructor continues the vanishing-bullseye technique, then demonstrates access on a training model. The paired sonogram shows a dark lumen with contour change and rebound as the instructor describes tenting, entry, and tracking the needle tip. He lowers and stabilizes the needle hand and begins removing the syringe. The demonstration is instructional and not a patient-specific outcome.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The schematic continues the vanishing-bullseye maneuver, with a target dot inside the vessel. The instructor says to repeat the adjustment until the needle hand can rest on the patient.
A slide titled ‘Vanishing Bullseye Technique: Advantages’ transitions to a hands-on probe-and-needle demonstration with an ultrasound view of a round dark lumen.
On a training model, the instructor advances a needle while scanning; the sonogram's round lumen changes contour and then rebounds as the instructor describes tenting and entry.

The probe and needle remain positioned over the training model as the instructor describes following the tip and adjusting the hand angle. The adjacent sonogram shows the dark lumen and a bright point.
The instructor lowers the needle hand until it can rest on the model and describes securing the needle between two fingers. The probe remains against the model; the sonogram shows a round lumen.
The hands-on demonstration continues with the probe hand stabilizing the model and the instructor beginning to remove the syringe. The segment is procedural teaching, not a patient outcome.

block_summary_target: The instructor emphasizes stabilizing the needle hand while handling the syringe or preparing a wire, then compares steep and shallow needle trajectories on a training model. He explains that a steep angle leaves less room before a through-and-through path, whereas a shallow angle provides more margin. The final split view shows an elongated dark channel with bright linear echoes as he discusses how needle visibility changes with probe angle; this is procedural teaching, not a patient-specific finding.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The instructor describes covering the needle with a sterile-gloved thumb after access and bracing the needle hand to limit movement during the procedure; the video shows hands working over the training model.
The instructor emphasizes keeping the needle hand braced while moving the syringe or preparing to pass a wire. The model and needle remain in view; no patient-specific result is shown.
The hands-on demonstration continues as the instructor considers how much needle movement is possible before problems occur; the probe and needle are positioned on the training model.
The instructor compares steep and shallow needle approaches on the training model, explaining that a steep angle leaves less room before the needle could cross the vessel.
The instructor says a shallower needle trajectory provides more distance before a through-and-through path and a greater margin for adjustment; the needle remains positioned on the model.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: A probe contacts the anterior upper chest of a supine patient, followed by a B-mode lung image with rib shadows and horizontal echoes. Narration introduces bedside lung ultrasound using the BLUE protocol for acute respiratory failure.

A rib-shadowed lung scan transitions through lower lateral chest probe placement to a deeper scan showing an anechoic space beside a solid organ. Narration describes BLUE as a rapid, systematic examination for identifying common causes of acute dyspnea.

A close view shows the transducer being positioned over the anterior chest. An on-screen teaching statement reports BLUE-protocol pneumonia sensitivity of 88% and specificity of 93% against a combined clinical, laboratory and CT reference standard.

The pneumonia-performance teaching slide remains briefly, then returns to anterior-chest scanning on the supine patient. Narration finishes describing the combined clinical, laboratory and CT reference standard for the reported BLUE-protocol performance.

Anterior chest scanning transitions to a labelled microconvex probe, then a side-by-side display of high-frequency linear and low-frequency curved probes. Narration introduces probe selection for the BLUE examination.

The labelled high-frequency linear and low-frequency curved probes are displayed, followed by a close view of the curved probe. Narration recommends using both high- and low-frequency probes when the preferred single probe is unavailable and introduces the low-frequency probe's assessment role.

block_summary_target: Labelled B-line and consolidation images illustrate low-frequency scanning, followed by a linear-probe pleural view as narration discusses assessing lung sliding. Six bilateral chest sites are then marked. Two palms demonstrate upper and lower anterior BLUE-point placement, and a lateral view introduces the third posterolateral assessment site with the arm raised.
global_summary_target: The BLUE-protocol tutorial introduces bedside assessment of acute dyspnea, probe selection and representative lung-ultrasound findings. It contrasts low-frequency artifact/consolidation imaging with a linear-probe pleural view, then maps six bilateral scanning sites using anterior hand landmarks and a lateral third point.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: Labelled examples change from B-lines, with bright vertical artifacts beneath the pleural region, to consolidation, with tissue-like echogenicity. Narration describes using the low-frequency probe to assess lung artifacts, consolidation and lung sliding.

A high-frequency linear probe is shown before a rectangular B-mode image displaying the bright pleural interface beneath chest-wall layers. Narration describes using this probe to assess lung sliding when it is unclear with the low-frequency probe.

Numbered BLUE scanning sites are illustrated on bilateral anterior chest views and a lateral raised-arm view with dashed landmark guides. Narration introduces six standardized scanning points, three on each side.
The examiner places two hands across the anterior chest with fingertips near the sternum. Narration describes using this hand position below the clavicle to locate the BLUE scanning points.

The hand-placement demonstration transitions back to numbered bilateral chest sites. Narration locates the upper BLUE point at the center of the upper palm and the lower point at the center of the lower palm.

The numbered chest map transitions to a lateral view with the arm raised, marking a third site and dashed guides from the lower anterior point. Narration introduces the posterolateral alveolar or pleural syndrome point alongside the anterior BLUE points.

block_summary_target: The third BLUE point is located using chest landmark guides before right upper anterior scanning begins with a curvilinear probe directed cephalad. The pleural line is shown between rib shadows while narration explains lung sliding. Subsequent annotated examples distinguish horizontal A-lines from vertical B-lines during low-frequency artifact assessment.
global_summary_target: The BLUE tutorial introduces acute-dyspnea assessment, probe selection and six bilateral scanning sites. Anterior palm landmarks and lateral guides locate the examination points. Right anterior scanning then demonstrates the pleural interface, explains lung sliding through narration, and uses annotated examples to distinguish A-lines from B-lines.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The curvilinear probe is placed on the lateral lower chest, followed by a numbered landmark diagram with dashed intersecting guides. Narration locates the third point using a horizontal line from the lower BLUE point and a line descending from the posterior axillary region.

The examiner begins on the patient's right anterior chest and places the curvilinear probe at the upper marked BLUE point. A close view shows the probe contacting the upper chest near the clavicle, matching narration introducing the right-sided scanning sequence.

Upper anterior chest probe placement transitions to a B-mode image showing a bright pleural line between two rib shadows. Narration directs the probe indicator toward the head and identifies this horizontal hyperechoic interface.

The B-mode pleural view continues between two rib shadows, with a caption identifying looped footage. Narration explains lung sliding as respiratory to-and-fro movement of visceral against parietal pleura.

The curvilinear probe remains at the upper anterior BLUE point, briefly shown beside the ultrasound depth scale. Narration directs assessment of A-lines, B-lines and consolidation with the low-frequency probe after checking lung sliding.

Annotated lung-ultrasound examples contrast A-lines, highlighted as regularly spaced horizontal reverberations parallel to the pleural line, with B-lines, highlighted as bright vertical artifacts. Narration describes the same distinction.

block_summary_target: A labelled consolidation example shows tissue-like lung, described in narration as hepatization. Probe placement progresses from the lower right anterior BLUE point to the posterolateral chest, then to the opposite hemithorax. A switch to the linear probe and a detailed pleural view illustrate troubleshooting when lung sliding is unclear.
global_summary_target: The BLUE tutorial has covered probe selection, bilateral chest landmarks, pleural-line identification and narrated lung-sliding assessment. Annotated A-line, B-line and consolidation examples accompany a scanning sequence from right anterior to posterolateral sites and then the left chest. Linear-probe imaging is introduced for equivocal sliding.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: A vertical-artifact lung image transitions to an annotated consolidation example, with a yellow outline around tissue-like echogenic lung. Narration describes B-lines originating at the pleura and consolidation as denser lung beneath an irregular pleural line.

A tissue-like lung example transitions to probe placement at the lower right anterior chest. Narration calls the liver-like appearance hepatization of the lung and then directs movement to the next anterior BLUE point.

The probe is shown at the lower right anterior chest and then farther laterally toward the posterior chest. Narration directs repeating the examination at the lower anterior point before moving posterolaterally to assess the right posterior lung.

Close views show the curved probe contacting the lateral lower chest and being repositioned. Narration directs placing it as far posteriorly as the patient's position permits for the posterior lung assessment.

The examiner reaches across to position the probe on the left chest of the supine patient. Narration directs repeating the sequence at the upper and lower left BLUE points and finally the left posterior lung region.
The examiner changes probes, followed by a high-frequency B-mode view of the chest wall and bright pleural interface. Narration recommends a linear probe when lung sliding is unclear or equivocal.

block_summary_target: Troubleshooting pairs probe tilting with pleural visualization and arm elevation with posterior access. C, A/B and B-prime teaching overlays describe pneumonia-associated consolidation and B-line distributions with sliding criteria. Paired consolidation and B-line examples are captioned with and without sliding.
global_summary_target: The BLUE-protocol tutorial combines bilateral chest scanning, probe selection, landmark placement and pleural/artifact identification. It adds troubleshooting for pleural visualization and posterior access, then explains pneumonia-associated C, A/B and B-prime teaching profiles through consolidation, B-line distribution and sliding criteria.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: A linear-probe pleural view transitions to a split view of probe contact and the lung image. Narration recommends slowly tilting the probe back and forth when the pleural line is not immediately visible.

The view changes from lung ultrasound to posterolateral chest probe placement with the arm raised. Narration recommends elevating the arm above the head, with assistance if needed, to improve access to the posterior lung.

Posterolateral probe placement gives way to a C-profile teaching overlay. The overlay defines any visualized consolidation, with or without lung sliding, as a profile that may indicate pneumonia; narration begins introducing these diagnostic profiles.

C-profile teaching text is followed by paired consolidation examples labelled with and without sliding, then A/B-profile criteria. The latter describes unilateral B-lines with either sliding state as potentially indicating pneumonia.

The A/B-profile criteria remain on screen before side-by-side B-line examples labelled with sliding and without sliding. The teaching overlay confines this profile to one hemithorax and allows either sliding state; the captions supply the motion interpretation.
Paired B-line examples are followed by a B-prime-profile teaching overlay describing bilateral B-lines without lung sliding as potentially indicating pneumonia.

block_summary_target: Teaching overlays distinguish bilateral B-lines with sliding in B-profile from A-profile with anterior sliding and A-lines. The A-profile pathway discusses posterior abnormalities and conditional leg-vein assessment for thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or obstructive disease. A-prime criteria then pair absent anterior sliding with A-lines as a reason to consider pneumothorax.
global_summary_target: The BLUE tutorial covers probe choice, six chest sites, bilateral anterior/posterior scanning, pleural-line visualization and A-line, B-line and consolidation examples. Teaching profiles relate artifact distribution and sliding to pneumonia or pulmonary-edema possibilities, and outline conditional A-profile/DVT assessment and A-prime pneumothorax consideration. These are instructional criteria rather than confirmed diagnoses in the demonstration patient.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The teaching overlay changes from B-prime to B-profile. B-profile is defined as bilateral B-lines with lung sliding and is described as potentially indicating pulmonary edema.

A split probe-and-ultrasound view labelled B-profile transitions to a scan with horizontal reverberations. Narration introduces the A-profile as lung sliding throughout the anterior fields with A-lines only.

Highlighted A-lines are followed by a transition toward posterior chest scanning and a deeper image containing an anechoic space beside a solid organ. Narration recommends posterior assessment after the anterior A-profile and discusses posterior B-lines or consolidation as suggestive of pneumonia.

An A-profile teaching overlay discusses posterior B-lines or consolidation as possible pneumonia signs. Narration gives the conditional next step when no abnormality is found: lower-extremity compression ultrasound to assess for deep venous thrombosis.

The A-profile teaching overlay presents a conditional diagnostic branch: deep venous thrombosis may indicate pulmonary embolism; when absent, obstructive airway disease such as COPD or asthma may be considered. Narration describes these possibilities without showing a leg-vein examination.

A lung-ultrasound example labelled A-prime profile is followed by its teaching criteria: absent anterior lung sliding with A-lines only. The overlay states that this pattern should prompt consideration of pneumothorax.

The A-prime criteria give way to a brief return to linear-probe chest scanning before the image fades to black. Closing narration states that BLUE has shown good diagnostic performance in acute respiratory failure.
No ultrasound-relevant visual information in this interval.
