The discussion then moves to the distal femur and proximal tibia, which are well seen on the sequence and can reveal lesions such as tumor, fracture, or infarction, before turning to cartilage. The lecture turns to cartilage, which appears as a gray layer between the bones but is not well visualized on standard MRI. Motamedi discusses research into improved cartilage imaging, including higher-field MRI and cartilage-mapping/post-processing methods that may reveal early loss before it is visible on routine images. He explains the clinical value of detecting cartilage loss because it cannot be restored once lost. The coronal knee MRI and anatomy checklist remain the visual context during this discussion. The presenter discusses cartilage restoration and preservation, including microfracture and cartilage implantation. These procedures may temporarily delay symptoms, but cartilage can wear again and repeat procedures or knee replacement may eventually be needed. The discussion then shifts to the meniscus, which absorbs hoop stress with each step; a torn meniscus may no longer distribute that load effectively. The coronal knee MRI remains the visual context. The presenter explains that cartilage loss can lead to increased stress on the underlying bone and may progress to total knee arthroplasty. The lecture then changes from coronal to axial (transverse) knee imaging and introduces an axial search pattern, moving from proximal to distal. The slide shows a patellofemoral joint diagram and lists retinaculum, cartilage, plica, ligaments/tendons, menisci, fluid collections, and loose bodies. The patellofemoral joint and some supporting structures are especially well assessed in this plane. The axial search pattern includes fluid collections, loose bodies, and soft-tissue abnormalities. A detailed labeled cross-sectional knee diagram is used to show the patella, femoral condyles, ligaments, tendons, and surrounding bursae. The presenter notes that the ACL and PCL can be seen in transverse section, though sagittal images show them more clearly along their long axes, then points out subcutaneous fat and the lateral femoral condyle. He begins reviewing bursae around the knee. Motamedi explains that a soft, fluctuant swelling over the knee may be a fluid-filled prepatellar bursa, particularly after repetitive kneeling, though infection or crystal deposition such as gout can also cause bursitis. He then turns to the patellofemoral joint. An axial knee MRI appears beside the axial search-pattern checklist as he identifies the patella and femur and describes assessing joint-space narrowing and degenerative change. The presenter concludes the basic imaging review by discussing a thickened plica, which may extend into cartilage and create clinically relevant defects. The axial search-pattern slide remains onscreen, then the lecture returns to an overview and transitions to sports-related knee abnormalities. The first topic is the ACL, introduced with a “Ligaments – Cruciate / ACL” slide and sagittal knee MRI. The ACL slide compares normal and abnormal sagittal MRI examples. The presenter identifies a torn ACL by abnormal high T2 signal and discontinuity, with a gap between fibers and edema or fluid in the ligament. A new “ACL Tear” slide states that acute rupture occurs about once per 3,000 people and is immediately disabling. The presenter begins describing a typical non-contact dynamic valgus mechanism. The presenter describes ACL injury mechanisms, including a non-contact twisting or dynamic valgus event and sudden change of direction or deceleration. The ACL tear slide reports approximately 50,000–175,000 reconstructions in the U.S. each year and identifies arthroscopic reconstruction as the standard for an ACL-deficient knee. A mechanism slide shows a football tackle and lists non-contact direction changes and deceleration, as well as clipping injuries in American football. Motamedi begins describing a force applied to a planted leg. The lecture compares ACL injury mechanisms in football and skiing. A football slide lists non-contact direction changes, deceleration, and clipping injuries; it adds sudden quadriceps contraction as a common skier mechanism. The presenter explains the pivot shift as the skier plants and turns, applying valgus stress. A new “ACL Tears – Pivot Shift Mechanism” slide shows knee diagrams and a skier, followed by a collage of football players and tackles. The presenter explains that ACL tears often occur when a person plants a foot and twists, sometimes with a valgus force. He notes that lifting the heel while twisting may reduce risk and distinguishes a sprain, where fibers remain continuous, from a full tear. After returning to football injury imagery, the lecture introduces secondary MRI signs of an ACL tear; the slide lists lateral-compartment bone bruising in 97% of cases. The presenter describes MRI findings that support an ACL tear beyond direct ligament inspection. The “ACL Tear – Secondary Signs” slide lists lateral-compartment bone bruising (97%), a deep lateral femoral notch greater than 1.5 mm, a second fracture, and PCL buckling. The lecture explains that anterior tibial translation can cause the tibia to strike the distal femur before returning to position, producing a pivot-shift bone contusion and sometimes an impaction fracture. A sagittal MRI illustrates the pivot-shift pattern. The presenter describes “kissing” bone contusions as a characteristic secondary sign of ACL injury. A large knee effusion can also support the diagnosis, especially when the ACL fibers are difficult to assess directly. The lecture notes that acute ACL injury is immediately disabling and often produces a large effusion. An “ACL Tear Secondary Signs – Deep Sulcus, Large Effusion” slide shows sagittal MRI examples; the presenter explains the deep femoral sulcus and bright marrow edema from bone impact. The presenter explains that imaging may be delayed 24 hours or longer after ACL injury so reactive effusion and bone marrow edema can develop and make the diagnosis clearer. He then describes a characteristic lateral tibial plateau avulsion/Segond fracture as another ACL-associated sign; the slide pairs a radiograph with coronal MRI. The lecture transitions to PCL tears, which the slide describes as less common than ACL tears in athletes, common in motor vehicle accidents, and associated with diffuse intermediate signal, discontinuity, and posterior tibial translation; conservative treatment is noted. The presenter explains that PCL tears are less common than ACL tears and usually result from a direct force that pushes the tibia posteriorly, often in a motor vehicle collision when the knee strikes a dashboard. The PCL tear slide lists diffuse intermediate signal, ligament discontinuity, and posterior tibial translation. MRI findings resemble those of an ACL tear but affect the PCL distribution and direction of tibial displacement. The presenter notes that even complete PCL tears are commonly managed conservatively. The presenter notes that adult PCL tears are commonly treated conservatively with bracing. A “Ligaments: PCL” slide compares sagittal MRI examples, including a disrupted PCL. The lecture shows football imagery while describing a running back who sustained a direct knee impact that translated the tibia posteriorly, noting that isolated PCL tears generally require substantial trauma. The presenter then changes topics to medial and lateral supporting structures, introducing the MCL with paired coronal MRI examples. A paired coronal MRI slide compares a normal MCL with a frankly abnormal ligament showing increased signal and discontinuity. The presenter notes that these basic MRI signs apply across ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL injuries. The lecture then introduces clinical MCL grades: Grade I stretch/sprain, Grade II partial tear with mild instability, and Grade III complete tear with significant instability. An accompanying diagram illustrates the injury grades, followed by the start of MRI grading. The presenter explains that Grade I and II MCL tears are often treated conservatively with bracing and activity modification, while surgery may be considered for complete tears in some highly active patients. The MRI grading slide defines Grade I as edema superficial to the MCL, Grade II as edema both superficial and deep to it, and Grade III as a complete tear. Coronal MRI examples illustrate Grade I and Grade II injuries, then transition to a Grade III example. The Grade III example shows a complete MCL tear with disorganized, retracted fibers and surrounding fluid. The presenter then explains that a later radiograph may show a small bone fleck from an old MCL injury. The “MCL Injury – Pellegrini-Stieda” slide pairs a focused knee radiograph with a coronal MRI and illustrates chronic injury-related ossification near the medial knee. The presenter contrasts chronic MCL changes on radiograph with acute MRI findings such as edema and fiber disruption. The lecture then moves to the lateral ligaments and iliotibial band. Coronal MRI examples show soft-tissue edema deep to the distal IT band near the lateral femoral condyle, consistent with iliotibial band friction syndrome. The presenter says it can cause lateral-sided pain in runners and is generally treated by limiting running and allowing rest. The lecture reviews the fibular collateral (lateral collateral) ligament, which runs from the femur to the proximal fibula. Coronal MRI examples contrast a normal low-signal ligament with hemorrhage and disorganized torn fibers. A second slide shows the biceps femoris tendon, another lateral supporting structure that inserts on the proximal fibula. Because these structures attach to the fibula, acute lateral injuries may avulse bone; the sequence ends with an “Arcuate Fracture” slide and paired MRI examples. The presenter compares MRI and radiographs for a subtle arcuate/avulsion fracture. The fragment can be difficult to see on MRI amid extensive ligament injury, but conspicuous on x-ray. He emphasizes obtaining radiographs alongside MRI and interpreting the studies together. The slide transitions from paired MRI examples to a radiograph showing the avulsed bone fragment. The lecture presents a severe knee dislocation case illustrated by a basketball player, radiograph, and MRI. The presenter explains that dislocations can tear multiple stabilizing ligaments, including the ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL, leaving little support around the knee. He discusses tibial displacement and notes that posterior displacement can injure the popliteal artery, making the injury potentially life-threatening. The lecture frames knee dislocation as a severe injury with potential vascular compromise. An ACR-style question asks which study beyond x-ray is the most appropriate initial imaging study, with choices including CT, MRI, and angiographic options; MRI is highlighted on the slide. The presenter emphasizes clinical pulse assessment because the popliteal artery may be injured, and says an absent pulse requires immediate surgical management. The presenter clarifies that acute knee dislocation management depends on palpable versus absent pulses; CT angiography may be used to map vessels before surgery, while MRI can evaluate associated injuries after stabilization. He summarizes the protocol, T1/T2 weighting, imaging planes, and knee anatomy covered so far. An overview slide returns, and the lecture shifts to meniscal injuries, which will occupy much of the remaining talk. The presenter introduces meniscal tear types and their treatment implications. A “Menisci – Normal ‘Bow Tie’ Sign” slide pairs a schematic with MRI, illustrating the normal low-signal meniscus. He identifies the anterior horn, body, and posterior horn on sagittal imaging and contrasts this with the perpendicular axial plane. The schematic and MRI remain onscreen as he explains how the structure appears across slices. The presenter explains that the meniscus appears as a low-signal bow tie on MRI, with anterior horn, body, and posterior horn visible in sagittal slices. A “Bow Tie Sign” slide says two body segments on 3 mm slices is normal, fewer than two can suggest a bucket-handle tear, and more than two can suggest a discoid meniscus. The lecture notes pitfalls such as a naturally small meniscus or prior surgery/resection. It then transitions to an “Abnormal” meniscus comparison. The lecture reviews an abnormal meniscus on MRI: increased signal in the posterior horn and a separated appearance indicate a frank tear. A slide compares normal and torn menisci and adds an arthroscopy view. The presenter describes how surgeons inspect the meniscus and may shave an unstable torn portion. The lecture then introduces tear categories with a diagram slide listing longitudinal (vertical, horizontal, oblique), bucket-handle, and radial tears, including parrot-beak. The presenter reviews meniscal tear types using a slide of schematics. Longitudinal tears are presented as common and may be vertical or horizontal; bucket-handle tears and less common radial tears are contrasted, with surgery noted for some cases. He then introduces tear examples, describing a linear longitudinal tear and a displaced bucket-handle fragment that can be felt during stepping and may cause clicking or catching. The lecture contrasts longitudinal and radial meniscal tears using a tear-types slide and presenter shots. A radial tear runs transversely from the free edge into the meniscal substance and is generally treated more aggressively because it can damage cartilage. The presenter explains the meniscus’s circumferential hoop stresses with a C-shaped diagram, setting up how a tear affects its load-distributing function. The presenter explains that radial tears disrupt circumferential meniscal hoop stresses, reducing load-bearing function and increasing the risk of cartilage degeneration. The tear-types slide illustrates parrot-beak and flap patterns; the presenter notes that displaced flap and bucket-handle fragments can need prompt treatment. The lecture then begins a vertical/oblique tear example, showing a sagittal MRI and identifying a linear longitudinal vertical tear. The lecture shows a vertical/oblique meniscal tear on sagittal MRI and discusses possible association with ACL-related instability as well as chronic degenerative wear; the presenter notes less inclination to operate on degenerative tears. A horizontal-tear slide then shows a marked MRI example, described as a linear tear along the posterior-to-anterior plane. The block ends with an abnormal grading slide contrasting intrasubstance degeneration and frank tear. The presenter distinguishes intrasubstance signal from a frank meniscal tear, which reaches an articular surface, using grading and MRI slides. The lecture then introduces bucket-handle tear signs: absent bow-tie, double PCL, and double anterior horn on sagittal imaging, plus a truncated meniscus and displaced fragment in the intercondylar notch on coronal imaging. A normal bow-tie slide transitions to an absent-bowtie example. The lecture demonstrates absent bow-tie and double-PCL signs of a bucket-handle tear. On the absent-bowtie slide, fluid occupies the expected second meniscal segment, providing an abnormal clue. A sagittal MRI then shows a displaced meniscal fragment in the intercondylar notch, paralleling the PCL and creating the double-PCL appearance. The presenter describes a bucket-handle tear and its surgical implications, then reviews a subtler coronal MRI example labeled “Fragment in Notch.” He compares normal and abnormal meniscal signal and notes that multiple findings can support the diagnosis. The lecture emphasizes understanding meniscal appearance across planes and transitions to an axial MRI example. The lecture reviews bucket-handle tear MRI appearances, including a displaced fragment in the notch, a ghost-meniscus appearance on sagittal images, and a double-PCL sign. It then introduces a flap tear with an illustration and coronal MRI, explaining that the displaced flap often lies in a medial or lateral gutter and may require surgery. The block ends with a radial-tear slide identifying the free edge and parrot-beak terminology. The lecture explains that a radial meniscal tear can cause peripheral extrusion, reducing meniscal coverage and increasing cartilage-on-cartilage loading as hoop-stress function is lost. The presenter links this to degeneration, osteoarthritis, and possible total knee arthroplasty. Slides show radial-tear terminology and treatment notes, then cleft and truncated-triangle MRI signs before introducing a peripheral-tear slide with red-zone, acute ACL, and anterior-translation notes. The lecture introduces meniscal cysts and shows coronal MRI examples, noting that a cyst in or adjacent to the meniscus suggests a tear. The presenter explains that joint fluid can track through the tear to form a cyst, which may be aspirated under ultrasound guidance with anesthetic and steroid; recurrent cysts may require surgical removal. The meniscus topic then closes, an overview slide appears, and the lecture begins a patellofemoral extensor section with a quadriceps tendon rupture MRI. The presenter reviews quadriceps and patellar tendon ruptures with sagittal MRI comparisons, showing tendon discontinuity and noting the acute clinical context and surrounding edema. The lecture then turns to cartilage imaging, showing sequence examples and a normal/abnormal patellar cartilage comparison, and introduces cartilage injury as relevant to preserving the joint and delaying arthroplasty. An osteochondral lesion example appears at the end. The lecture defines an osteochondral lesion as an abnormality involving both bone and cartilage, showing arrow-marked examples and a four-view MRI panel. The presenter explains that an intact, nondisplaced fragment may be anchored to preserve the overlying cartilage and stresses early detection before displacement. A cartilage fissure MRI slide appears as the lecture moves to synovial plicae.

The OCL slide remains visible while the presenter explains that a nondisplaced lesion may be surgically anchored to preserve the overlying cartilage.
The slide transitions to a four-image MRI panel illustrating the osteochondral lesion across multiple views.
The four-view MRI panel remains onscreen as the presenter points out abnormal bone and overlying articular cartilage.
The presenter continues the osteochondral-lesion discussion at the lectern; a Cartilage – Fissure slide appears near the end, just before the discussion turns to synovial plicae.
The presentation changes to a “Cartilage – Fissure” slide with an axial knee MRI while the presenter begins discussing synovial plicae.

The presenter shows a football injury case with corresponding knee MRI and radiographs, emphasizing the value of radiographs alongside MRI. The segment ends with a review question asking viewers to identify an MRI plane.

A UCSF Osher Center for Integrative Medicine title sequence shows monochrome healthcare and community imagery, identifies the Mini Medical School for the Public, and introduces a radiology and biomedical imaging program before landing on the title “Sports Medicine Imaging, Musculoskeletal Ultrasound and Ultrasound-Guided Procedures.” The attributed opening narration is a UCTV station promotion and does not yet describe the clinical presentation. A UCSF title card identifies Daria Motamedi, MD, and Tara Morgan, MD. Motamedi then appears at a lectern and introduces “Imaging Common Sports Related Injuries,” followed by a short lecture introduction. The first teaching slide begins with “Question 1” and a sagittal knee MRI. The attributed narration identifies Motamedi’s musculoskeletal imaging specialty, introduces the sports-injury imaging topic and says Tara Morgan will speak next about musculoskeletal ultrasound. The opening quiz uses three knee MRI slides. Question 1 asks viewers to identify the imaging plane and lists sagittal, coronal, axial, and none of the above. Question 2 shows a different MRI and asks viewers to identify the sequence, with T1, T2, and fat-suppressed options. Question 3 shows another knee MRI and asks which injury is depicted, listing ACL, PCL, medial collateral ligament, and medial meniscal tears. The presenter appears at the lectern between questions. The attributed narration walks through each prompt and says the lecture will explain the answers. The overview slide lists the lecture sequence: protocol, anatomy/search pattern, ligaments, menisci, patellofemoral extensor mechanism, cartilage, and other topics. Motamedi explains that the talk will cover knee anatomy, ligaments, common meniscal tears and their treatment, the extensor mechanism, and cartilage. The sequence ends by beginning the imaging protocol section with a sagittal T2 fat-suppressed knee MRI. The knee MRI protocol slide builds a set of standard sequences: sagittal T2 fat-suppressed and sagittal T1, followed by coronal T1 and coronal T2 fat-suppressed images, then an axial T2 fat-suppressed image. The presenter explains the sagittal, coronal, and axial planes and notes that fat suppression makes subcutaneous fat dark, while fluid is bright on T2 and fat is bright on T1. The sequence returns to a sagittal image for comparison. After completing the protocol discussion, the lecture moves to an “Anatomy / Search Pattern – Sagittal” slide. A knee illustration accompanies a checklist of ligaments (ACL and PCL), posterolateral corner, menisci, patellofemoral extensor mechanism, bones, and cartilage. The presenter explains the sagittal search pattern, including the distal quadriceps tendon, patellar tendon, patellar aponeurosis, and anterior bursae, then begins reviewing a sagittal knee MRI and identifies the fibula as a lateral landmark. The presenter uses sagittal knee MRI slices to explain a lateral-to-medial search pattern. The fibular head marks the lateral side. He then reviews the meniscus, describing its anterior horn, body, and posterior horn as locations used to report tears. The sequence moves to cruciate ligament anatomy, introducing the ACL and its role in anterior stability of the knee. The sagittal anatomy checklist remains visible throughout. The sagittal knee MRI is used to review ligament anatomy. The presenter describes ACL function and clinical testing, then points out the low-signal ACL and its femoral and tibial attachments. The PCL lies just behind it and contributes to posterior stability. The review shifts to the medial meniscus, whose anterior horn, body, and posterior horn are described, before the presenter returns to the quadriceps and patellar tendons and begins explaining the quadriceps tendon’s components. Motamedi explains the extensor mechanism using the sagittal knee anatomy view. The quadriceps tendon contains four tendinous contributions, so its distal signal may reflect normal tendon confluence rather than a tear. He then describes the patellar tendon from the patella to the tibial tuberosity, discussing patellar tendon tears and traction apophysitis in adolescents and athletes with pain at the insertion. The patellar tendon is also relevant to ACL surgery because a bone–patellar tendon–bone graft is commonly used for reconstruction. The sagittal MRI review reinforces that fluid is bright on T2, fat is bright on T1, and dark subcutaneous fat identifies a T2 fat-suppressed sequence, commonly used for sports imaging. The presenter then introduces coronal imaging as a front-facing view through the knee, progressing anterior to posterior rather than lateral to medial. The lecture moves to a coronal anatomy/search-pattern slide with a knee illustration and checklist of the MCL, LCL complex, menisci, bones, and cartilage. The lecture uses the coronal knee anatomy slide to discuss the supporting structures best seen in this plane. The MCL and LCL complex are listed, with the lateral complex including the lateral collateral ligament, iliotibial band, and biceps femoris tendon. The presenter describes iliotibial band friction syndrome, in which the distal IT band and adjacent soft tissues can become inflamed near the lateral femoral condyle, and notes conservative treatment. The coronal view also shows the menisci from anterior to posterior. The coronal anatomy review covers meniscal root attachments and shows the distal femur, medial and lateral femoral condyles, tibial plateau, and proximal fibula. The fibula identifies the lateral side. Motamedi then explains that the knee comprises three articulations: medial femorotibial, lateral femorotibial, and patellofemoral compartments. The coronal slide remains as he introduces cartilage between the bones. The lecture transitions from the coronal knee illustration to MRI examples. The presenter points out that coronal views show the distal quadriceps tendon, patella, and patellar tendon, and introduces a T2 fat-suppressed sequence progressing from anterior to posterior. He explains that the extensor tendons can be assessed for tears or tendinosis, then begins identifying lateral structures, starting with the iliotibial band. The coronal MRI review finishes the lateral side, including the LCL and tendinous attachments at the proximal fibula. The presenter then turns to the medial side, where the MCL is the main structure. It appears as a low-signal band; fluid around it or visible discontinuity would be abnormal. The discussion then moves to the distal femur and proximal tibia, which are well seen on the sequence and can reveal lesions such as tumor, fracture, or infarction, before turning to cartilage. The lecture turns to cartilage, which appears as a gray layer between the bones but is not well visualized on standard MRI. Motamedi discusses research into improved cartilage imaging, including higher-field MRI and cartilage-mapping/post-processing methods that may reveal early loss before it is visible on routine images. He explains the clinical value of detecting cartilage loss because it cannot be restored once lost. The coronal knee MRI and anatomy checklist remain the visual context during this discussion. The presenter discusses cartilage restoration and preservation, including microfracture and cartilage implantation. These procedures may temporarily delay symptoms, but cartilage can wear again and repeat procedures or knee replacement may eventually be needed. The discussion then shifts to the meniscus, which absorbs hoop stress with each step; a torn meniscus may no longer distribute that load effectively. The coronal knee MRI remains the visual context. The presenter explains that cartilage loss can lead to increased stress on the underlying bone and may progress to total knee arthroplasty. The lecture then changes from coronal to axial (transverse) knee imaging and introduces an axial search pattern, moving from proximal to distal. The slide shows a patellofemoral joint diagram and lists retinaculum, cartilage, plica, ligaments/tendons, menisci, fluid collections, and loose bodies. The patellofemoral joint and some supporting structures are especially well assessed in this plane. The axial search pattern includes fluid collections, loose bodies, and soft-tissue abnormalities. A detailed labeled cross-sectional knee diagram is used to show the patella, femoral condyles, ligaments, tendons, and surrounding bursae. The presenter notes that the ACL and PCL can be seen in transverse section, though sagittal images show them more clearly along their long axes, then points out subcutaneous fat and the lateral femoral condyle. He begins reviewing bursae around the knee. Motamedi explains that a soft, fluctuant swelling over the knee may be a fluid-filled prepatellar bursa, particularly after repetitive kneeling, though infection or crystal deposition such as gout can also cause bursitis. He then turns to the patellofemoral joint. An axial knee MRI appears beside the axial search-pattern checklist as he identifies the patella and femur and describes assessing joint-space narrowing and degenerative change. The presenter concludes the basic imaging review by discussing a thickened plica, which may extend into cartilage and create clinically relevant defects. The axial search-pattern slide remains onscreen, then the lecture returns to an overview and transitions to sports-related knee abnormalities. The first topic is the ACL, introduced with a “Ligaments – Cruciate / ACL” slide and sagittal knee MRI. The ACL slide compares normal and abnormal sagittal MRI examples. The presenter identifies a torn ACL by abnormal high T2 signal and discontinuity, with a gap between fibers and edema or fluid in the ligament. A new “ACL Tear” slide states that acute rupture occurs about once per 3,000 people and is immediately disabling. The presenter begins describing a typical non-contact dynamic valgus mechanism. The presenter describes ACL injury mechanisms, including a non-contact twisting or dynamic valgus event and sudden change of direction or deceleration. The ACL tear slide reports approximately 50,000–175,000 reconstructions in the U.S. each year and identifies arthroscopic reconstruction as the standard for an ACL-deficient knee. A mechanism slide shows a football tackle and lists non-contact direction changes and deceleration, as well as clipping injuries in American football. Motamedi begins describing a force applied to a planted leg. The lecture compares ACL injury mechanisms in football and skiing. A football slide lists non-contact direction changes, deceleration, and clipping injuries; it adds sudden quadriceps contraction as a common skier mechanism. The presenter explains the pivot shift as the skier plants and turns, applying valgus stress. A new “ACL Tears – Pivot Shift Mechanism” slide shows knee diagrams and a skier, followed by a collage of football players and tackles. The presenter explains that ACL tears often occur when a person plants a foot and twists, sometimes with a valgus force. He notes that lifting the heel while twisting may reduce risk and distinguishes a sprain, where fibers remain continuous, from a full tear. After returning to football injury imagery, the lecture introduces secondary MRI signs of an ACL tear; the slide lists lateral-compartment bone bruising in 97% of cases. The presenter describes MRI findings that support an ACL tear beyond direct ligament inspection. The “ACL Tear – Secondary Signs” slide lists lateral-compartment bone bruising (97%), a deep lateral femoral notch greater than 1.5 mm, a second fracture, and PCL buckling. The lecture explains that anterior tibial translation can cause the tibia to strike the distal femur before returning to position, producing a pivot-shift bone contusion and sometimes an impaction fracture. A sagittal MRI illustrates the pivot-shift pattern. The presenter describes “kissing” bone contusions as a characteristic secondary sign of ACL injury. A large knee effusion can also support the diagnosis, especially when the ACL fibers are difficult to assess directly. The lecture notes that acute ACL injury is immediately disabling and often produces a large effusion. An “ACL Tear Secondary Signs – Deep Sulcus, Large Effusion” slide shows sagittal MRI examples; the presenter explains the deep femoral sulcus and bright marrow edema from bone impact. The presenter explains that imaging may be delayed 24 hours or longer after ACL injury so reactive effusion and bone marrow edema can develop and make the diagnosis clearer. He then describes a characteristic lateral tibial plateau avulsion/Segond fracture as another ACL-associated sign; the slide pairs a radiograph with coronal MRI. The lecture transitions to PCL tears, which the slide describes as less common than ACL tears in athletes, common in motor vehicle accidents, and associated with diffuse intermediate signal, discontinuity, and posterior tibial translation; conservative treatment is noted. The presenter explains that PCL tears are less common than ACL tears and usually result from a direct force that pushes the tibia posteriorly, often in a motor vehicle collision when the knee strikes a dashboard. The PCL tear slide lists diffuse intermediate signal, ligament discontinuity, and posterior tibial translation. MRI findings resemble those of an ACL tear but affect the PCL distribution and direction of tibial displacement. The presenter notes that even complete PCL tears are commonly managed conservatively. The presenter notes that adult PCL tears are commonly treated conservatively with bracing. A “Ligaments: PCL” slide compares sagittal MRI examples, including a disrupted PCL. The lecture shows football imagery while describing a running back who sustained a direct knee impact that translated the tibia posteriorly, noting that isolated PCL tears generally require substantial trauma. The presenter then changes topics to medial and lateral supporting structures, introducing the MCL with paired coronal MRI examples. A paired coronal MRI slide compares a normal MCL with a frankly abnormal ligament showing increased signal and discontinuity. The presenter notes that these basic MRI signs apply across ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL injuries. The lecture then introduces clinical MCL grades: Grade I stretch/sprain, Grade II partial tear with mild instability, and Grade III complete tear with significant instability. An accompanying diagram illustrates the injury grades, followed by the start of MRI grading. The presenter explains that Grade I and II MCL tears are often treated conservatively with bracing and activity modification, while surgery may be considered for complete tears in some highly active patients. The MRI grading slide defines Grade I as edema superficial to the MCL, Grade II as edema both superficial and deep to it, and Grade III as a complete tear. Coronal MRI examples illustrate Grade I and Grade II injuries, then transition to a Grade III example. The Grade III example shows a complete MCL tear with disorganized, retracted fibers and surrounding fluid. The presenter then explains that a later radiograph may show a small bone fleck from an old MCL injury. The “MCL Injury – Pellegrini-Stieda” slide pairs a focused knee radiograph with a coronal MRI and illustrates chronic injury-related ossification near the medial knee. The presenter contrasts chronic MCL changes on radiograph with acute MRI findings such as edema and fiber disruption. The lecture then moves to the lateral ligaments and iliotibial band. Coronal MRI examples show soft-tissue edema deep to the distal IT band near the lateral femoral condyle, consistent with iliotibial band friction syndrome. The presenter says it can cause lateral-sided pain in runners and is generally treated by limiting running and allowing rest. The lecture reviews the fibular collateral (lateral collateral) ligament, which runs from the femur to the proximal fibula. Coronal MRI examples contrast a normal low-signal ligament with hemorrhage and disorganized torn fibers. A second slide shows the biceps femoris tendon, another lateral supporting structure that inserts on the proximal fibula. Because these structures attach to the fibula, acute lateral injuries may avulse bone; the sequence ends with an “Arcuate Fracture” slide and paired MRI examples. The presenter compares MRI and radiographs for a subtle arcuate/avulsion fracture. The fragment can be difficult to see on MRI amid extensive ligament injury, but conspicuous on x-ray. He emphasizes obtaining radiographs alongside MRI and interpreting the studies together. The slide transitions from paired MRI examples to a radiograph showing the avulsed bone fragment. The lecture presents a severe knee dislocation case illustrated by a basketball player, radiograph, and MRI. The presenter explains that dislocations can tear multiple stabilizing ligaments, including the ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL, leaving little support around the knee. He discusses tibial displacement and notes that posterior displacement can injure the popliteal artery, making the injury potentially life-threatening. The lecture frames knee dislocation as a severe injury with potential vascular compromise. An ACR-style question asks which study beyond x-ray is the most appropriate initial imaging study, with choices including CT, MRI, and angiographic options; MRI is highlighted on the slide. The presenter emphasizes clinical pulse assessment because the popliteal artery may be injured, and says an absent pulse requires immediate surgical management. The presenter clarifies that acute knee dislocation management depends on palpable versus absent pulses; CT angiography may be used to map vessels before surgery, while MRI can evaluate associated injuries after stabilization. He summarizes the protocol, T1/T2 weighting, imaging planes, and knee anatomy covered so far. An overview slide returns, and the lecture shifts to meniscal injuries, which will occupy much of the remaining talk. The presenter introduces meniscal tear types and their treatment implications. A “Menisci – Normal ‘Bow Tie’ Sign” slide pairs a schematic with MRI, illustrating the normal low-signal meniscus. He identifies the anterior horn, body, and posterior horn on sagittal imaging and contrasts this with the perpendicular axial plane. The schematic and MRI remain onscreen as he explains how the structure appears across slices. The presenter explains that the meniscus appears as a low-signal bow tie on MRI, with anterior horn, body, and posterior horn visible in sagittal slices. A “Bow Tie Sign” slide says two body segments on 3 mm slices is normal, fewer than two can suggest a bucket-handle tear, and more than two can suggest a discoid meniscus. The lecture notes pitfalls such as a naturally small meniscus or prior surgery/resection. It then transitions to an “Abnormal” meniscus comparison. The lecture reviews an abnormal meniscus on MRI: increased signal in the posterior horn and a separated appearance indicate a frank tear. A slide compares normal and torn menisci and adds an arthroscopy view. The presenter describes how surgeons inspect the meniscus and may shave an unstable torn portion. The lecture then introduces tear categories with a diagram slide listing longitudinal (vertical, horizontal, oblique), bucket-handle, and radial tears, including parrot-beak. The presenter reviews meniscal tear types using a slide of schematics. Longitudinal tears are presented as common and may be vertical or horizontal; bucket-handle tears and less common radial tears are contrasted, with surgery noted for some cases. He then introduces tear examples, describing a linear longitudinal tear and a displaced bucket-handle fragment that can be felt during stepping and may cause clicking or catching. The lecture contrasts longitudinal and radial meniscal tears using a tear-types slide and presenter shots. A radial tear runs transversely from the free edge into the meniscal substance and is generally treated more aggressively because it can damage cartilage. The presenter explains the meniscus’s circumferential hoop stresses with a C-shaped diagram, setting up how a tear affects its load-distributing function. The presenter explains that radial tears disrupt circumferential meniscal hoop stresses, reducing load-bearing function and increasing the risk of cartilage degeneration. The tear-types slide illustrates parrot-beak and flap patterns; the presenter notes that displaced flap and bucket-handle fragments can need prompt treatment. The lecture then begins a vertical/oblique tear example, showing a sagittal MRI and identifying a linear longitudinal vertical tear. The lecture shows a vertical/oblique meniscal tear on sagittal MRI and discusses possible association with ACL-related instability as well as chronic degenerative wear; the presenter notes less inclination to operate on degenerative tears. A horizontal-tear slide then shows a marked MRI example, described as a linear tear along the posterior-to-anterior plane. The block ends with an abnormal grading slide contrasting intrasubstance degeneration and frank tear. The presenter distinguishes intrasubstance signal from a frank meniscal tear, which reaches an articular surface, using grading and MRI slides. The lecture then introduces bucket-handle tear signs: absent bow-tie, double PCL, and double anterior horn on sagittal imaging, plus a truncated meniscus and displaced fragment in the intercondylar notch on coronal imaging. A normal bow-tie slide transitions to an absent-bowtie example. The lecture demonstrates absent bow-tie and double-PCL signs of a bucket-handle tear. On the absent-bowtie slide, fluid occupies the expected second meniscal segment, providing an abnormal clue. A sagittal MRI then shows a displaced meniscal fragment in the intercondylar notch, paralleling the PCL and creating the double-PCL appearance. The presenter describes a bucket-handle tear and its surgical implications, then reviews a subtler coronal MRI example labeled “Fragment in Notch.” He compares normal and abnormal meniscal signal and notes that multiple findings can support the diagnosis. The lecture emphasizes understanding meniscal appearance across planes and transitions to an axial MRI example. The lecture reviews bucket-handle tear MRI appearances, including a displaced fragment in the notch, a ghost-meniscus appearance on sagittal images, and a double-PCL sign. It then introduces a flap tear with an illustration and coronal MRI, explaining that the displaced flap often lies in a medial or lateral gutter and may require surgery. The block ends with a radial-tear slide identifying the free edge and parrot-beak terminology. The lecture explains that a radial meniscal tear can cause peripheral extrusion, reducing meniscal coverage and increasing cartilage-on-cartilage loading as hoop-stress function is lost. The presenter links this to degeneration, osteoarthritis, and possible total knee arthroplasty. Slides show radial-tear terminology and treatment notes, then cleft and truncated-triangle MRI signs before introducing a peripheral-tear slide with red-zone, acute ACL, and anterior-translation notes. The lecture introduces meniscal cysts and shows coronal MRI examples, noting that a cyst in or adjacent to the meniscus suggests a tear. The presenter explains that joint fluid can track through the tear to form a cyst, which may be aspirated under ultrasound guidance with anesthetic and steroid; recurrent cysts may require surgical removal. The meniscus topic then closes, an overview slide appears, and the lecture begins a patellofemoral extensor section with a quadriceps tendon rupture MRI. The presenter reviews quadriceps and patellar tendon ruptures with sagittal MRI comparisons, showing tendon discontinuity and noting the acute clinical context and surrounding edema. The lecture then turns to cartilage imaging, showing sequence examples and a normal/abnormal patellar cartilage comparison, and introduces cartilage injury as relevant to preserving the joint and delaying arthroplasty. An osteochondral lesion example appears at the end. The lecture defines an osteochondral lesion as an abnormality involving both bone and cartilage, showing arrow-marked examples and a four-view MRI panel. The presenter explains that an intact, nondisplaced fragment may be anchored to preserve the overlying cartilage and stresses early detection before displacement. A cartilage fissure MRI slide appears as the lecture moves to synovial plicae. The lecture closes the cartilage section, including plica-related fissures and anterior knee pain, then moves to bone marrow. A fracture slide notes that fractures are best seen on T1 and marrow edema on T2. The presenter shows a football injury case with corresponding knee MRI and radiographs, emphasizing the value of radiographs alongside MRI. The segment ends with a review question asking viewers to identify an MRI plane. The lecture reviews imaging planes and sequences with two quiz slides. Question 1 shows a knee MRI and asks for the imaging plane; the presenter identifies it as sagittal. Question 2 reuses the double-PCL bucket-handle example and asks for the sequence. Bright joint fluid indicates T2 weighting, and suppressed dark fat identifies a T2 fat-suppressed sagittal sequence. The final quiz slide shows a sagittal fluid-sensitive MRI with a large knee effusion and asks which injury is present; the presenter identifies an ACL tear and thanks the audience. The thank-you slide remains during the close, after which the presenter introduces a second speaker, Tara Morgan, and transitions to musculoskeletal ultrasound as a growing imaging technique. The first presenter closes his remarks on musculoskeletal ultrasound, noting its growth and possible use before shoulder MRI for reimbursement. He introduces Tara Morgan, who begins a talk titled “Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (How cool is this?!)” The lower third identifies her as Tara A. Morgan, MD, UCSF Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging. She opens with a personal comment about ACL injury. Tara Morgan introduces her enthusiasm for musculoskeletal ultrasound and frames the talk around its role in evaluating the musculoskeletal system. A take-home slide asks why the technique is not more widely used. She begins with ultrasound basics, showing the machine and explaining the transducer and gel interface, and highlights that ultrasound uses sound waves without radiation. Morgan describes ultrasound as portable and useful at the bedside, including 3D capability and vascular information. A slide shows several transducer types, which are selected based on the examination. The presentation then lists ultrasound advantages: it is fast, readily available, cost effective, and useful for guiding procedures. Morgan highlights ultrasound’s real-time procedural guidance without radiation and its ability to show small structures at high resolution. The advantages slide adds ultrasound as an alternative or adjunct to MRI, particularly when implanted hardware is incompatible or creates MRI artifact, and in pregnancy as an initial imaging approach.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The “Pros of Ultrasound” slide remains visible while Morgan describes real-time image-guided needle placement without radiation to the patient or clinician.
The slide adds increased resolution for small anatomy as Morgan explains that ultrasound can depict tiny structures in detail.
The advantages slide adds that ultrasound can serve as an alternative or adjunct to MRI.
The slide lists situations where ultrasound can help: MRI-incompatible hardware and hardware-related MRI artifacts.
Morgan continues explaining ultrasound’s usefulness when metal hardware limits MRI visualization; the expanded advantages slide remains on screen.
The slide adds pregnancy as another situation where ultrasound may be a useful initial imaging approach.

block_summary_target: Morgan shows a pregnant patient’s left and right piriformis ultrasound views; the symptomatic left piriformis appears enlarged, supporting diagnosis without MRI. She then introduces dynamic ultrasound: real-time scanning can localize a patient’s pain and capture movement, which is useful for position-dependent conditions such as hernia.

A new “ACL Tear” slide states that acute rupture occurs about once per 3,000 people and is immediately disabling. The presenter begins describing a typical non-contact dynamic valgus mechanism. The presenter describes ACL injury mechanisms, including a non-contact twisting or dynamic valgus event and sudden change of direction or deceleration. The ACL tear slide reports approximately 50,000–175,000 reconstructions in the U.S. each year and identifies arthroscopic reconstruction as the standard for an ACL-deficient knee. A mechanism slide shows a football tackle and lists non-contact direction changes and deceleration, as well as clipping injuries in American football. Motamedi begins describing a force applied to a planted leg. The lecture compares ACL injury mechanisms in football and skiing. A football slide lists non-contact direction changes, deceleration, and clipping injuries; it adds sudden quadriceps contraction as a common skier mechanism. The presenter explains the pivot shift as the skier plants and turns, applying valgus stress. A new “ACL Tears – Pivot Shift Mechanism” slide shows knee diagrams and a skier, followed by a collage of football players and tackles. The presenter explains that ACL tears often occur when a person plants a foot and twists, sometimes with a valgus force. He notes that lifting the heel while twisting may reduce risk and distinguishes a sprain, where fibers remain continuous, from a full tear. After returning to football injury imagery, the lecture introduces secondary MRI signs of an ACL tear; the slide lists lateral-compartment bone bruising in 97% of cases. The presenter describes MRI findings that support an ACL tear beyond direct ligament inspection. The “ACL Tear – Secondary Signs” slide lists lateral-compartment bone bruising (97%), a deep lateral femoral notch greater than 1.5 mm, a second fracture, and PCL buckling. The lecture explains that anterior tibial translation can cause the tibia to strike the distal femur before returning to position, producing a pivot-shift bone contusion and sometimes an impaction fracture. A sagittal MRI illustrates the pivot-shift pattern. The presenter describes “kissing” bone contusions as a characteristic secondary sign of ACL injury. A large knee effusion can also support the diagnosis, especially when the ACL fibers are difficult to assess directly. The lecture notes that acute ACL injury is immediately disabling and often produces a large effusion. An “ACL Tear Secondary Signs – Deep Sulcus, Large Effusion” slide shows sagittal MRI examples; the presenter explains the deep femoral sulcus and bright marrow edema from bone impact. The presenter explains that imaging may be delayed 24 hours or longer after ACL injury so reactive effusion and bone marrow edema can develop and make the diagnosis clearer. He then describes a characteristic lateral tibial plateau avulsion/Segond fracture as another ACL-associated sign; the slide pairs a radiograph with coronal MRI. The lecture transitions to PCL tears, which the slide describes as less common than ACL tears in athletes, common in motor vehicle accidents, and associated with diffuse intermediate signal, discontinuity, and posterior tibial translation; conservative treatment is noted. The presenter explains that PCL tears are less common than ACL tears and usually result from a direct force that pushes the tibia posteriorly, often in a motor vehicle collision when the knee strikes a dashboard. The PCL tear slide lists diffuse intermediate signal, ligament discontinuity, and posterior tibial translation. MRI findings resemble those of an ACL tear but affect the PCL distribution and direction of tibial displacement. The presenter notes that even complete PCL tears are commonly managed conservatively. The presenter notes that adult PCL tears are commonly treated conservatively with bracing. A “Ligaments: PCL” slide compares sagittal MRI examples, including a disrupted PCL. The lecture shows football imagery while describing a running back who sustained a direct knee impact that translated the tibia posteriorly, noting that isolated PCL tears generally require substantial trauma. The presenter then changes topics to medial and lateral supporting structures, introducing the MCL with paired coronal MRI examples. A paired coronal MRI slide compares a normal MCL with a frankly abnormal ligament showing increased signal and discontinuity. The presenter notes that these basic MRI signs apply across ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL injuries. The lecture then introduces clinical MCL grades: Grade I stretch/sprain, Grade II partial tear with mild instability, and Grade III complete tear with significant instability. An accompanying diagram illustrates the injury grades, followed by the start of MRI grading. The presenter explains that Grade I and II MCL tears are often treated conservatively with bracing and activity modification, while surgery may be considered for complete tears in some highly active patients. The MRI grading slide defines Grade I as edema superficial to the MCL, Grade II as edema both superficial and deep to it, and Grade III as a complete tear. Coronal MRI examples illustrate Grade I and Grade II injuries, then transition to a Grade III example. The Grade III example shows a complete MCL tear with disorganized, retracted fibers and surrounding fluid. The presenter then explains that a later radiograph may show a small bone fleck from an old MCL injury. The “MCL Injury – Pellegrini-Stieda” slide pairs a focused knee radiograph with a coronal MRI and illustrates chronic injury-related ossification near the medial knee. The presenter contrasts chronic MCL changes on radiograph with acute MRI findings such as edema and fiber disruption. The lecture then moves to the lateral ligaments and iliotibial band. Coronal MRI examples show soft-tissue edema deep to the distal IT band near the lateral femoral condyle, consistent with iliotibial band friction syndrome. The presenter says it can cause lateral-sided pain in runners and is generally treated by limiting running and allowing rest. The lecture reviews the fibular collateral (lateral collateral) ligament, which runs from the femur to the proximal fibula. Coronal MRI examples contrast a normal low-signal ligament with hemorrhage and disorganized torn fibers. A second slide shows the biceps femoris tendon, another lateral supporting structure that inserts on the proximal fibula. Because these structures attach to the fibula, acute lateral injuries may avulse bone; the sequence ends with an “Arcuate Fracture” slide and paired MRI examples. The presenter compares MRI and radiographs for a subtle arcuate/avulsion fracture. The fragment can be difficult to see on MRI amid extensive ligament injury, but conspicuous on x-ray. He emphasizes obtaining radiographs alongside MRI and interpreting the studies together. The slide transitions from paired MRI examples to a radiograph showing the avulsed bone fragment. The lecture presents a severe knee dislocation case illustrated by a basketball player, radiograph, and MRI. The presenter explains that dislocations can tear multiple stabilizing ligaments, including the ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL, leaving little support around the knee. He discusses tibial displacement and notes that posterior displacement can injure the popliteal artery, making the injury potentially life-threatening. The lecture frames knee dislocation as a severe injury with potential vascular compromise. An ACR-style question asks which study beyond x-ray is the most appropriate initial imaging study, with choices including CT, MRI, and angiographic options; MRI is highlighted on the slide. The presenter emphasizes clinical pulse assessment because the popliteal artery may be injured, and says an absent pulse requires immediate surgical management. The presenter clarifies that acute knee dislocation management depends on palpable versus absent pulses; CT angiography may be used to map vessels before surgery, while MRI can evaluate associated injuries after stabilization. He summarizes the protocol, T1/T2 weighting, imaging planes, and knee anatomy covered so far. An overview slide returns, and the lecture shifts to meniscal injuries, which will occupy much of the remaining talk. The presenter introduces meniscal tear types and their treatment implications. A “Menisci – Normal ‘Bow Tie’ Sign” slide pairs a schematic with MRI, illustrating the normal low-signal meniscus. He identifies the anterior horn, body, and posterior horn on sagittal imaging and contrasts this with the perpendicular axial plane. The schematic and MRI remain onscreen as he explains how the structure appears across slices. The presenter explains that the meniscus appears as a low-signal bow tie on MRI, with anterior horn, body, and posterior horn visible in sagittal slices. A “Bow Tie Sign” slide says two body segments on 3 mm slices is normal, fewer than two can suggest a bucket-handle tear, and more than two can suggest a discoid meniscus. The lecture notes pitfalls such as a naturally small meniscus or prior surgery/resection. It then transitions to an “Abnormal” meniscus comparison. The lecture reviews an abnormal meniscus on MRI: increased signal in the posterior horn and a separated appearance indicate a frank tear. A slide compares normal and torn menisci and adds an arthroscopy view. The presenter describes how surgeons inspect the meniscus and may shave an unstable torn portion. The lecture then introduces tear categories with a diagram slide listing longitudinal (vertical, horizontal, oblique), bucket-handle, and radial tears, including parrot-beak. The presenter reviews meniscal tear types using a slide of schematics. Longitudinal tears are presented as common and may be vertical or horizontal; bucket-handle tears and less common radial tears are contrasted, with surgery noted for some cases. He then introduces tear examples, describing a linear longitudinal tear and a displaced bucket-handle fragment that can be felt during stepping and may cause clicking or catching. The lecture contrasts longitudinal and radial meniscal tears using a tear-types slide and presenter shots. A radial tear runs transversely from the free edge into the meniscal substance and is generally treated more aggressively because it can damage cartilage. The presenter explains the meniscus’s circumferential hoop stresses with a C-shaped diagram, setting up how a tear affects its load-distributing function. The presenter explains that radial tears disrupt circumferential meniscal hoop stresses, reducing load-bearing function and increasing the risk of cartilage degeneration. The tear-types slide illustrates parrot-beak and flap patterns; the presenter notes that displaced flap and bucket-handle fragments can need prompt treatment. The lecture then begins a vertical/oblique tear example, showing a sagittal MRI and identifying a linear longitudinal vertical tear. The lecture shows a vertical/oblique meniscal tear on sagittal MRI and discusses possible association with ACL-related instability as well as chronic degenerative wear; the presenter notes less inclination to operate on degenerative tears. A horizontal-tear slide then shows a marked MRI example, described as a linear tear along the posterior-to-anterior plane. The block ends with an abnormal grading slide contrasting intrasubstance degeneration and frank tear. The presenter distinguishes intrasubstance signal from a frank meniscal tear, which reaches an articular surface, using grading and MRI slides. The lecture then introduces bucket-handle tear signs: absent bow-tie, double PCL, and double anterior horn on sagittal imaging, plus a truncated meniscus and displaced fragment in the intercondylar notch on coronal imaging. A normal bow-tie slide transitions to an absent-bowtie example. The lecture demonstrates absent bow-tie and double-PCL signs of a bucket-handle tear. On the absent-bowtie slide, fluid occupies the expected second meniscal segment, providing an abnormal clue. A sagittal MRI then shows a displaced meniscal fragment in the intercondylar notch, paralleling the PCL and creating the double-PCL appearance. The presenter describes a bucket-handle tear and its surgical implications, then reviews a subtler coronal MRI example labeled “Fragment in Notch.” He compares normal and abnormal meniscal signal and notes that multiple findings can support the diagnosis. The lecture emphasizes understanding meniscal appearance across planes and transitions to an axial MRI example. The lecture reviews bucket-handle tear MRI appearances, including a displaced fragment in the notch, a ghost-meniscus appearance on sagittal images, and a double-PCL sign. It then introduces a flap tear with an illustration and coronal MRI, explaining that the displaced flap often lies in a medial or lateral gutter and may require surgery. The block ends with a radial-tear slide identifying the free edge and parrot-beak terminology. The lecture explains that a radial meniscal tear can cause peripheral extrusion, reducing meniscal coverage and increasing cartilage-on-cartilage loading as hoop-stress function is lost. The presenter links this to degeneration, osteoarthritis, and possible total knee arthroplasty. Slides show radial-tear terminology and treatment notes, then cleft and truncated-triangle MRI signs before introducing a peripheral-tear slide with red-zone, acute ACL, and anterior-translation notes. The lecture introduces meniscal cysts and shows coronal MRI examples, noting that a cyst in or adjacent to the meniscus suggests a tear. The presenter explains that joint fluid can track through the tear to form a cyst, which may be aspirated under ultrasound guidance with anesthetic and steroid; recurrent cysts may require surgical removal. The meniscus topic then closes, an overview slide appears, and the lecture begins a patellofemoral extensor section with a quadriceps tendon rupture MRI. The presenter reviews quadriceps and patellar tendon ruptures with sagittal MRI comparisons, showing tendon discontinuity and noting the acute clinical context and surrounding edema. The lecture then turns to cartilage imaging, showing sequence examples and a normal/abnormal patellar cartilage comparison, and introduces cartilage injury as relevant to preserving the joint and delaying arthroplasty. An osteochondral lesion example appears at the end. The lecture defines an osteochondral lesion as an abnormality involving both bone and cartilage, showing arrow-marked examples and a four-view MRI panel. The presenter explains that an intact, nondisplaced fragment may be anchored to preserve the overlying cartilage and stresses early detection before displacement. A cartilage fissure MRI slide appears as the lecture moves to synovial plicae. The lecture closes the cartilage section, including plica-related fissures and anterior knee pain, then moves to bone marrow. A fracture slide notes that fractures are best seen on T1 and marrow edema on T2. The presenter shows a football injury case with corresponding knee MRI and radiographs, emphasizing the value of radiographs alongside MRI. The segment ends with a review question asking viewers to identify an MRI plane. The lecture reviews imaging planes and sequences with two quiz slides. Question 1 shows a knee MRI and asks for the imaging plane; the presenter identifies it as sagittal. Question 2 reuses the double-PCL bucket-handle example and asks for the sequence. Bright joint fluid indicates T2 weighting, and suppressed dark fat identifies a T2 fat-suppressed sagittal sequence. The final quiz slide shows a sagittal fluid-sensitive MRI with a large knee effusion and asks which injury is present; the presenter identifies an ACL tear and thanks the audience. The thank-you slide remains during the close, after which the presenter introduces a second speaker, Tara Morgan, and transitions to musculoskeletal ultrasound as a growing imaging technique. The first presenter closes his remarks on musculoskeletal ultrasound, noting its growth and possible use before shoulder MRI for reimbursement. He introduces Tara Morgan, who begins a talk titled “Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (How cool is this?!)” The lower third identifies her as Tara A. Morgan, MD, UCSF Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging. She opens with a personal comment about ACL injury. Tara Morgan introduces her enthusiasm for musculoskeletal ultrasound and frames the talk around its role in evaluating the musculoskeletal system. A take-home slide asks why the technique is not more widely used. She begins with ultrasound basics, showing the machine and explaining the transducer and gel interface, and highlights that ultrasound uses sound waves without radiation. Morgan describes ultrasound as portable and useful at the bedside, including 3D capability and vascular information. A slide shows several transducer types, which are selected based on the examination. The presentation then lists ultrasound advantages: it is fast, readily available, cost effective, and useful for guiding procedures. Morgan highlights ultrasound’s real-time procedural guidance without radiation and its ability to show small structures at high resolution. The advantages slide adds ultrasound as an alternative or adjunct to MRI, particularly when implanted hardware is incompatible or creates MRI artifact, and in pregnancy as an initial imaging approach. Morgan shows a pregnant patient’s left and right piriformis ultrasound views; the symptomatic left piriformis appears enlarged, supporting diagnosis without MRI. She then introduces dynamic ultrasound: real-time scanning can localize a patient’s pain and capture movement, which is useful for position-dependent conditions such as hernia.

The review shifts to the medial meniscus, whose anterior horn, body, and posterior horn are described, before the presenter returns to the quadriceps and patellar tendons and begins explaining the quadriceps tendon’s components. Motamedi explains the extensor mechanism using the sagittal knee anatomy view. The quadriceps tendon contains four tendinous contributions, so its distal signal may reflect normal tendon confluence rather than a tear. He then describes the patellar tendon from the patella to the tibial tuberosity, discussing patellar tendon tears and traction apophysitis in adolescents and athletes with pain at the insertion. The presenter then introduces coronal imaging as a front-facing view through the knee, progressing anterior to posterior rather than lateral to medial. The lecture uses the coronal knee anatomy slide to discuss the supporting structures best seen in this plane. The presenter describes iliotibial band friction syndrome, in which the distal IT band and adjacent soft tissues can become inflamed near the lateral femoral condyle, and notes conservative treatment. The coronal view also shows the menisci from anterior to posterior. The coronal anatomy review covers meniscal root attachments and shows the distal femur, medial and lateral femoral condyles, tibial plateau, and proximal fibula. The coronal slide remains as he introduces cartilage between the bones. The lecture transitions from the coronal knee illustration to MRI examples. The presenter points out that coronal views show the distal quadriceps tendon, patella, and patellar tendon, and introduces a T2 fat-suppressed sequence progressing from anterior to posterior. He explains that the extensor tendons can be assessed for tears or tendinosis, then begins identifying lateral structures, starting with the iliotibial band. The coronal MRI review finishes the lateral side, including the LCL and tendinous attachments at the proximal fibula. The presenter then turns to the medial side, where the MCL is the main structure. It appears as a low-signal band; fluid around it or visible discontinuity would be abnormal. The discussion then moves to the distal femur and proximal tibia, which are well seen on the sequence and can reveal lesions such as tumor, fracture, or infarction, before turning to cartilage. The lecture turns to cartilage, which appears as a gray layer between the bones but is not well visualized on standard MRI. Motamedi discusses research into improved cartilage imaging, including higher-field MRI and cartilage-mapping/post-processing methods that may reveal early loss before it is visible on routine images. He explains the clinical value of detecting cartilage loss because it cannot be restored once lost. The coronal knee MRI and anatomy checklist remain the visual context during this discussion. The presenter discusses cartilage restoration and preservation, including microfracture and cartilage implantation. These procedures may temporarily delay symptoms, but cartilage can wear again and repeat procedures or knee replacement may eventually be needed. The discussion then shifts to the meniscus, which absorbs hoop stress with each step; a torn meniscus may no longer distribute that load effectively. The coronal knee MRI remains the visual context. The presenter explains that cartilage loss can lead to increased stress on the underlying bone and may progress to total knee arthroplasty. The lecture then changes from coronal to axial (transverse) knee imaging and introduces an axial search pattern, moving from proximal to distal. He begins reviewing bursae around the knee. He then turns to the patellofemoral joint. The lecture transitions to PCL tears, which the slide describes as less common than ACL tears in athletes, common in motor vehicle accidents, and associated with diffuse intermediate signal, discontinuity, and posterior tibial translation; conservative treatment is noted. The PCL tear slide lists diffuse intermediate signal, ligament discontinuity, and posterior tibial translation. MRI findings resemble those of an ACL tear but affect the PCL distribution and direction of tibial displacement. The presenter notes that even complete PCL tears are commonly managed conservatively. The presenter notes that adult PCL tears are commonly treated conservatively with bracing. A “Ligaments: PCL” slide compares sagittal MRI examples, including a disrupted PCL. The lecture shows football imagery while describing a running back who sustained a direct knee impact that translated the tibia posteriorly, noting that isolated PCL tears generally require substantial trauma. The presenter then changes topics to medial and lateral supporting structures, introducing the MCL with paired coronal MRI examples. The presenter notes that these basic MRI signs apply across ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL injuries. An accompanying diagram illustrates the injury grades, followed by the start of MRI grading. Coronal MRI examples illustrate Grade I and Grade II injuries, then transition to a Grade III example. The presenter then explains that a later radiograph may show a small bone fleck from an old MCL injury.
