The presenter describes MRI findings that support an ACL tear beyond direct ligament inspection. The “ACL Tear – Secondary Signs” slide lists lateral-compartment bone bruising (97%), a deep lateral femoral notch greater than 1.5 mm, a second fracture, and PCL buckling. The lecture explains that anterior tibial translation can cause the tibia to strike the distal femur before returning to position, producing a pivot-shift bone contusion and sometimes an impaction fracture. A sagittal MRI illustrates the pivot-shift pattern. The presenter describes “kissing” bone contusions as a characteristic secondary sign of ACL injury. A large knee effusion can also support the diagnosis, especially when the ACL fibers are difficult to assess directly. The lecture notes that acute ACL injury is immediately disabling and often produces a large effusion. An “ACL Tear Secondary Signs – Deep Sulcus, Large Effusion” slide shows sagittal MRI examples; the presenter explains the deep femoral sulcus and bright marrow edema from bone impact. The presenter explains that imaging may be delayed 24 hours or longer after ACL injury so reactive effusion and bone marrow edema can develop and make the diagnosis clearer. He then describes a characteristic lateral tibial plateau avulsion/Segond fracture as another ACL-associated sign; the slide pairs a radiograph with coronal MRI. The lecture transitions to PCL tears, which the slide describes as less common than ACL tears in athletes, common in motor vehicle accidents, and associated with diffuse intermediate signal, discontinuity, and posterior tibial translation; conservative treatment is noted. The presenter explains that PCL tears are less common than ACL tears and usually result from a direct force that pushes the tibia posteriorly, often in a motor vehicle collision when the knee strikes a dashboard. The PCL tear slide lists diffuse intermediate signal, ligament discontinuity, and posterior tibial translation. MRI findings resemble those of an ACL tear but affect the PCL distribution and direction of tibial displacement. The presenter notes that even complete PCL tears are commonly managed conservatively. The presenter notes that adult PCL tears are commonly treated conservatively with bracing. A “Ligaments: PCL” slide compares sagittal MRI examples, including a disrupted PCL. The lecture shows football imagery while describing a running back who sustained a direct knee impact that translated the tibia posteriorly, noting that isolated PCL tears generally require substantial trauma. The presenter then changes topics to medial and lateral supporting structures, introducing the MCL with paired coronal MRI examples. A paired coronal MRI slide compares a normal MCL with a frankly abnormal ligament showing increased signal and discontinuity. The presenter notes that these basic MRI signs apply across ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL injuries. Morgan then introduces bone as a dense, highly calcified structure: ultrasound shows a bright surface but cannot image deeply through it. Although bone shape varies, its surface should be smooth; the lecture ends this interval with a normal Achilles tendon and calcaneus ultrasound example. Morgan shows normal bone ultrasound at the Achilles insertion on the calcaneus and at the finger phalanges, emphasizing the smooth bright cortical surface. A bone-pathology slide lists fracture, infection, arthritis, tumor, and hardware abnormality. She highlights plastic orthopedic screws as hardware that may be visible with ultrasound, including screws from her own ACL repair. Morgan compares acute and healing fractures on ultrasound: an acute fracture produces an abrupt cortical step-off, while healing bone becomes irregular and fluffy. The lecture then presents a large thigh soft-tissue mass; the underlying femoral surface appears irregular rather than smoothly contoured, suggesting a bone reaction associated with the mass. After identifying the thigh mass as lymphoma, Morgan introduces muscle and its tendon attachment to bone. She demonstrates normal calf muscle in transverse ultrasound, distinguishing the gastrocnemius and deeper soleus above the tibia and fibula. Morgan outlines muscle pathology, including tear, hematoma, mass, infection/inflammation, infarction, and atrophy, then explains the brighter fatty replacement associated with infarction or atrophy. A partial calf muscle tear is illustrated with a dark fluid-like gap and surrounding bleed. The segment then changes to T1 and fat-suppressed T2 MRI views of a right-thigh mass. The ultrasound-guided thigh-mass biopsy is shown with paired FNA and core-biopsy images and identified as a low-grade tumor requiring removal. The lecture then shifts to tendons and ligaments: a slide shows tendon attaching muscle to bone and ligament attaching bone to bone, while the narration describes their parallel, rope-like appearance and common injury or inflammation. Morgan explains that tendon insertions can experience stress and become symptomatic. A “Normal Achilles Tendon” slide pairs a longitudinal ultrasound view with an anatomical illustration; the narration describes parallel fibers without focal thickening or signal loss and follows the tendon to its calcaneal insertion. The lecture then transitions to a rotator-cuff tendon ultrasound at the shoulder. A rotator-cuff ultrasound marks the tendon’s shoulder-bone attachment; the narration notes that fluid or a missing segment can indicate a tear. A labeled supraspinatus tendon view shows a broad attachment described as normal. The lecture then lists tendon pathology, including tenosynovitis, tendinosis and partial or complete tears, before introducing a patient with right-arm pain and visible asymmetry. A distal biceps tendon rupture slide pairs an elbow ultrasound with an anatomical diagram; the narration confirms the tendon was torn, describes retraction under tension, and notes the normal radial insertion is absent more distally. The lecture then introduces a favorite case with wrist radiographs showing fixation plates and screws from a prior fracture, followed by a new fall on an outstretched hand and movement difficulty. The wrist radiographs show existing fixation plates and screws without a protruding screw. A longitudinal wrist-tendon ultrasound labels tendon and bone, then highlights a screw extending beyond the bone margin toward the tendon. A transverse comparison shows the right-sided tendon is roughly twice the size of the left. A transverse wrist comparison shows enlargement of the affected tendon, and color Doppler shows increased flow around it. An operative photograph shows tendon and hardware exposure as the protruding screw is removed and the tendon repaired; Morgan then returns to the lectern and introduces nerves. The lecture then introduces peripheral nerves and their motor and sensory functions, describing the honeycomb appearance and nerve sheaths alongside a median-nerve wrist ultrasound. A following slide presents the labeled median nerve in the carpal tunnel. Morgan then shows transverse median-nerve ultrasound at the carpal tunnel, a sciatic-nerve scan, and a “Nerve vs. Tendon” comparison that labels the myotendinous junction and median nerve. Morgan then reviews nerve entrapment, dislocation, and tumors. A carpal-tunnel slide maps the median-nerve distribution and labeled tunnel contents, followed by a normal-versus-abnormal ultrasound comparison showing a visibly enlarged, fascicular median nerve. The final minute compares normal and abnormal median-nerve ultrasound, then presents the lecture’s conclusion: musculoskeletal ultrasound has unique advantages, can support diagnosis and treatment, and can add to patient care. A “Thank you!” slide closes the talk before audience questions. During audience Q&A, Morgan explains that mammography is used for broad screening while ultrasound provides higher detail for small structures, complements X-rays but is harder for deep targets, and can assess a mammographic abnormality and guide biopsy. During the following audience questions, Morgan says ultrasound has almost no long-term effects, though higher power can theoretically heat tissue and this is considered in pregnancy; she says it is rarely a concern in adults. The discussion then turns to MRI scanner space and noise. Daria Motamedi, identified on screen, describes MRI noise and mentions earplugs and headphones. During the following Q&A, Motamedi discusses MRI noise, targeted wrist and knee coils, claustrophobia, scanner weight limits, and larger-bore MRI availability. The interval shows both presenters at the lectern without clinical imaging. Motamedi answers a question about open MRI, noting lower signal-to-noise and reduced image quality compared with closed scanners, with some fine detail potentially not visible. The presenters conclude the Q&A, and the video shows UCSF Osher Center closing slates for the Mini Medical School and the Radiology & Biomedical Imaging program, naming Daria Motamedi and Tara Morgan.
